#3353. Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

The AI pioneer says it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big issues

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he says he has identified the next big shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Ng’s current efforts are focused on his company Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he says can yield “small data” solutions to big issues in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

The great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

Andrew Ng: This is a big question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having said that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

Ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a new paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Having said that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of users, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing company with millions of users.

Ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

“In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI

I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and said, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

Over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing new here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and said, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

The data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one company or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that showed up.

You often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

When you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand new model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

Ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having said that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For big data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng

For example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very quickly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

Ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. New tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an important piece of the puzzle.

One of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Ng: In AI, data cleaning is important, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention quickly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

For example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Ng: I think synthetic data is an important tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

Ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

“In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng

Synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

To make these issues more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a company approaches Landing AI and says it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

One of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

How do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

Ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift issue. I find it really important to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and update the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

Ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent new neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s important for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

Ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print issue as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor, where she helps develop and shape the magazine’s longform stories. She also oversees Spectrum's coverage of artificial intelligence and biomedical engineering. She holds a master’s degree in journalism from Columbia University.

There’s plenty to watch across the major streaming services this week, but some movies and shows won’t be sticking around for much longer. From Netflix and Prime Video to Hulu and HBO Max, several titles are preparing to leave their respective platforms over the next few days.

That means it’s time to check your watchlist and see if there’s anything you’ve been putting off. I’ve rounded up 40 movies and shows worth catching before they disappear, including a few hidden gems, familiar favorites and titles you might have missed the first time around.

Whether you’re after a gripping horror flick, a compelling crime film, or something a little more romantic, there’s plenty to choose from. So, if any of these have been sitting on your watchlist, now might be the time to watch before they’re gone.

What it's about: Medical student Nancy Adams (Blake Lively) travels to a secluded Mexican beach to surf, but her relaxing getaway takes a terrifying turn when a great white shark attacks her. Injured and stranded on a small rock just 200 yards from shore, Nancy must find a way back to land while the predator circles nearby. With limited supplies, rising tides and no immediate help, she faces a desperate fight to survive.

Why you should watch it: "The Shallows" is a great choice when you're after a tense survival thriller that gets straight to the action. Blake Lively carries the film with a convincing physical performance, while director Jaume Collet-Serra makes the most of its isolated setting and terrifying underwater encounters. There's very little padding here, with the 87-minute runtime keeping the story focused and the tension consistently high. It's a particularly good watch if you enjoy shark movies.

Watch "The Shallows" on Netflix until Nov. 15

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

What it's about: Once a radical revolutionary, Bob Ferguson (Leonardo DiCaprio) has settled into an isolated life, raising his teenage daughter, Willa (Chase Infiniti), away from the world. But when his former nemesis, Colonel Steven J. Lockjaw (Sean Penn), resurfaces after 16 years and Willa mysteriously disappears, Bob is forced back into action. Desperate to find his daughter, he reconnects with former allies and confronts the dangerous consequences of his past.

Why you should watch it: There's a lot going on in "One Battle After Another," but that's exactly what makes it such an entertaining watch. Paul Thomas Anderson throws Leonardo DiCaprio into a chaotic story full of outrageous situations, explosive action and some genuinely funny moments. Sean Penn is particularly good as the film's menacing antagonist, providing a strong foil to DiCaprio's character. The unpredictable plot and standout performances give you plenty of reasons to stick around until the end.

Watch "One Battle After Another" on Prime Video until Nov. 18

What it's about: In "Twisters," former storm chaser Kate Carter (Daisy Edgar-Jones) returns to Oklahoma at the request of an old friend to test a new tornado-tracking system. There, she crosses paths with Tyler Owens (Glen Powell), a reckless social media star who chases storms with his crew. As an unprecedented tornado outbreak threatens the region, the rival teams must work together to survive increasingly destructive weather.

Why you should watch it: Few disaster movies deliver quite as much spectacle as "Twisters." The tornado sequences are easily the biggest draw, with some impressive visual effects and genuinely nerve-racking moments as the characters find themselves caught in the path of increasingly dangerous storms. Daisy Edgar-Jones and Glen Powell make an enjoyable leading pair, bringing enough charm and humor to balance out all the destruction.

#3351. What to Expect From Best Buy's 2026 Black Friday and Cyber Monday Sales

For all intents and purposes, Black Friday sales are already here. There are plenty of deals out already, even though we're weeks away from the actual event. One of the reasons for that is the competition retailers have with each other to be the first to get your money. One of the retailers that is making the biggest early splash is Best Buy, confirming their entire plan for the rest of the year. Here's what you need to know.

Best Buy has announced the following events:

DoorBoosters: A Halloween sale from Oct. 30 to Nov. 1.

Early Black Friday Deals and Doorbusters: The official start of early Black Friday deals on Nov. 6. New deals will drop every Friday.

Black Friday Doorbusters and Deals: Best Buy says this will be its main sale, starting on Thursday, Nov. 19 and running until Nov. 28 with deals on "computing, gaming, home theater, wearables, and more."

Cyber Sunday and Monday: Best Buy is extending Cyber Monday to five days and says you can find deals going up to 50% off select tech.

Last-minute savings: The Christmas sale will run from Dec. 18 until Dec. 24.

You don't need to be any kind of member to shop Best Buy's Black Friday in July sale; however, it is free to sign up for a My Best Buy membership, which will get you free shipping. If you join one of their paid subscriptions (My Best Buy Plus for $49.99 per year or My Best Buy Total for $179.99 per year), you'll get faster free shipping, exclusive prices and deals, an extended 60-day return window on most products, and access to select sales, like the Member Deals Days sale that is going on right now. Paid members will also earn extra rewards from both the current sale and the upcoming Black Friday in July sale.

You can find deals on TVs, laptops, headphones, video games, electric bikes, and more. There will be new deals every week in stores, on its website, and in the Best Buy mobile app. They'll offer price matching, meaning if the price drops further during the sale (Dec. 24), they will match it and offer a refund.

Here are the best deals I've found so far. I'll be updating these deals throughout the sale, so make sure to come back and see what's new. Remember that new deals drop every day.

Best Buy price matches its own products, so if a product drops in price later, you'd get those savings too, but it does not cover any deals coming from a competitor's Black Friday sale. There are some other important exceptions you can read in more detail here.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

The other major retailers doing Black Friday sales are Amazon, Target, and Walmart. Currently, Amazon has many early deals, seeing their lowest prices yet. Target has some week-long deals and a Deal of the Day. Walmart will have three Black Friday and Cyber Monday shopping events. Nowadays, large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

#3350. Spotify’s AI DJ adds nine voices and a setting to reduce interruptions

Spotify today expanded customization options for its AI DJ, allowing users to choose between different voices and personalities, as well as control how much the DJ talks between songs. Here are the details.

If you’re not familiar with Spotify’s AI DJ feature, the company describes it as “a personalized mix of music and commentary to help you discover new favorites and connect more deeply with the artists you love,” adding that it takes your listening history into account to “[bring] together your favorite tracks, songs you haven’t heard in years, and new releases to keep things feeling fresh.”

Spotify first introduced the interactive version of DJ in May 2025, and soon expanded its capabilities to Spanish-speaking users. Then, last May, Spotify expanded availability to more than 75 countries, alongside support for French, German, Italian, and Brazilian Portuguese.

Now, as spotted by TechCrunch, Spotify is introducing more customization options, including new voices and personalities, as well as the ability to reduce commentary between songs.

In a new post published on Spotify’s For the Record blog, the company announced today that “Spotify Premium listeners in markets where DJ is available can choose from an expanded selection of DJ voices in English and Spanish,” with seven new English options spanning British, American, Irish, Australian, and Indian accents, along with two new Spanish voices.

Additionally, Spotify now lets users choose whether they want commentary between sets of songs through a toggle that reduces the DJ’s interruptions to brief acknowledgments when starting a session or requesting different music.

Spotify also shared a carousel on Instagram with short audio previews of each new DJ voice, giving users a chance to hear how they sound:

#3349. Watch Rosalía Bring Operatic Flair to Latin Grammys Performance

Rosalía has officially returned to the Latin Grammys stage. The Spanish superstar brought all of the drama when she emerged from a smoke-covered stage wearing a gold gown surrounding by a flank of dancers.

Rosalía embodied a sun goddess as she sang three songs, starting with “La Rumba Del Perdón” before diving into fan-favorite “La Perla” and finishing off with the sassy write-off “Dios Es Un Stalker.” Just before she belted out the final note in that song, she took a moment to commemorate the night. “Welcome to the Latin Grammys,” Rosalía told the audience. “Tonight is to enjoy yourself.”

🚨| ROSALÍA interpreta «La Rumba Del Perdón», «La Perla» y «Dios Es Un Stalker (Versión Francotiradora)» en una actuación espectacular con la que da comienzo a la ceremonia de los Latin Grammy 2026. pic.twitter.com/mGRQGvF3il

This year, Rosalía is up for her fourth album Lux, which earned seven nods including Album of the Year, Song of the Year, and Best Pop Song. The Spanish singer is also up for Best Portuguese Language Song for Lux cut “Memória.” Portuguese is one of the 14 languages Rosalía employed on the album. The singer has earned 11 overall Latin Grammys in her career.

It marks the Spanish artist’s first performance at the Latin Grammys in three years. Back in 2023, when the ceremony was hosted in her homeland of Spain, Rosalía delivered a soulful rendition of Rocío Jurado’s ballad “Se Nos Rompió El Amor.” She hasn’t performed an original song at the Latin Grammys since her pop-forward offering of “Despecha” in 2022. #3348. The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build

Agility Robotics’ first practical robotic worker is nothing like I dreamed

Author and Agility Robotics co-founder Jonathan Hurst next to his new Digit 5 humanoid robot worker.

Agility Robotics, the company I cofounded out of my robotics lab at Oregon State University in 2015, has just launched Digit 5. It’s designed to be the first humanoid robot that can safely and economically do useful work at scale, allowing us to bring tens of thousands of humanoid workers into the real world. Engineered to lift 23-kilogram bins onto high shelves and with a battery that can run for 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge, Digit 5’s goal is to handle heavy warehouse tasks shift after shift, filling the need for labor in jobs that are too physically stressful or too dull for humans to want to do.

Digit 5 is what Agility has been working toward for over a decade. But the robot is heavy and bulky, lacking the graceful natural motion of its predecessors, and it’s farther than I thought possible from the robot I dreamed of building when I started this company. To deliver a useful commercial product, Agility has taken a path that is very different from what I first imagined.

My dream has always been to build robots that combine locomotion and manipulation to move through the world and interact with it as people do. I seek a mastery of motion, achieved through devices designed to navigate the constraints of physics with elegance. When I started the Dynamic Robotics Laboratory at Oregon State in 2008, we began with a theory derived from decades of work in biomechanics: that a simple “spring-mass” model (a body supported by legs that act like springs) should be able to reproduce every known walking and running gait found in animals.

We put theory into practice by building the bipedal robot ATRIAS—short for “Assume The Robot Is A Sphere,” a joke among physicists about reducing a complex system to its simplest possible form. ATRIAS looked like a large microwave on stilts because it was only intended to demonstrate the physics of human walking and running. This was the first glimmer of achieving my dream; even though ATRIAS wasn’t designed to look like us, it still seemed natural, and even somehow alive, when it settled into a walking gait.

With the success of ATRIAS, the barriers to progress shifted from scientific to engineering and organizational, and a startup company seemed like the way to bridge the gap from a one-off research concept to an actual robotic product. I felt confident of two things: that I would be able to build robots that could go where people go, and that this capability would be incredibly useful. This combination of ambition and naivete is necessary for anyone to found a new company—how hard could it be?

Good advice for starting a company is to understand a customer problem, and then find a way to solve it using your unique capabilities. My cofounders, Damion Shelton and Mikhail Jones, and I did not do this. We relied on our belief that this technology would enable new possibilities and trusted ourselves to figure out the business as we went. So we simply focused on building our first product: the bipedal robot Cassie.

Cassie was the first dynamic bipedal robot that researchers could buy, able to maintain its balance through active, fluid motion rather than careful, rigid steps. It had ostrichlike legs, not because we were imitating ground-running birds, but as a result of engineering strictly for performance. It was not intended to be commercially useful, and had no torso, arms, or head. We sold Cassie robots to Harvard, Caltech, the University of Michigan, the University of California, Berkeley, and a handful of other research institutions, ultimately saturating the market for US $250,000 bipedal research robots after having sold a total of 10 of them.

ATRIAS, Cassie, and Digit 4 EVT [left to right] are on display at Agility Robotics’ RoboFab in Salem, Ore. The 70,000-square-foot facility has the capacity to produce more than 10,000 Digit 5 robots per year.Agility Robotics

Because Cassie’s hardware enabled research into the physics of walking and running, the legged-robot research frontier shifted to control software. Traditionally, engineers controlled legged robots with detailed mathematical models that determined how the machines should move. With Cassie, researchers pioneered the new approach of reinforcement learning for bipedal legged locomotion: A simulated robot learns through trial and error, and the resulting neural network controls the physical machine. This approach is what enables virtually all of the dynamic behaviors that you see on legged robots today, and Cassie looked alive as it recovered from stumbles while climbing stairs, ran 5 kilometers across the Oregon State campus, and broke the robot world record for a 100-meter dash.

Cassie got us closer to being able to move through the world with confidence and grace, but to make it useful, we needed manipulation. After exhaustively exploring different configurations, we found that an upright torso helped the robot balance, while two arms mounted near the top of the torso allowed it to pick up large objects and to catch itself when it fell. Digit 1, which added a torso and arms to the Cassie legs, was our first mobile manipulation robot, and another step on the path toward a product that could do useful work for commercial customers.

As we explored the first applications for Digit, potential customers kept asking us: Why legs? And why a humanoid? These were tough questions for me to answer, because they exposed a core business reality: It didn’t matter to Agility Robotics if we solved a cool science problem in a beautiful way. What mattered to the business was solving real problems for customers.

After years of engagement with industry partners, we found one answer in warehouses and manufacturing facilities: moving bins. Bin handling is a clearly defined task where two arms are needed to lift large bins up high and legs are the best way to balance and move in narrow spaces. Because the task can vary widely from one deployment to another, it hasn’t been broadly addressed by single-purpose automation. Yet it was constrained enough to give Digit an economically viable first job while it developed a broader set of skills.

In 2019, Digit began demonstrating its capabilities to do real work. With Ford Motor Company, we showed how Digit 1 could carry packages from an autonomous vehicle to a front porch. We developed Digit 2 and 3 while working with a certain global package delivery company on moving and sorting cardboard boxes. Amazon tested Digit 4 on moving and stacking bins, and it became the world’s first commercially deployed humanoid at the logistics provider GXO. In 2024, Digit appeared on the cover of Time magazine.

Despite Digit’s apparent success, we began to run into conflicts between my dream and the needs of actual customers. We were no longer working with relatively patient university research labs. Agility has to sell robots to survive, and customers will only purchase robots that provide value. If bins weren’t moving, our customers were losing money. We spent a huge amount of time and effort keeping our first deployments operational, which arguably eliminated any profit we made. Yet this also kept our company learning and alive the way no lab demo ever could.

I had no idea how hard it would be, or that running a company would involve so many things that have nothing to do with solving technical problems: deployments across the country; shipping, service, and customer support; fundraising and investor relations; more fundraising; human resources and IT; developing fleet-management software; managing a supply chain; and even more fundraising. I had no experience with any of these things. My career had focused on solving the technical challenges of robots interacting with the world, and it turned out that was only a tiny piece of building a successful robotics company. But Agility was the only path I saw to continuing the technical work and having an impact.

I knew that Agility needed to focus more on robots as a product, but I didn’t know how to make that happen. Hiring the people we needed to run the company meant giving up an immense amount of control, but we had no other choice. We recruited a new executive team with the experience required to commercialize this new technology, and they quickly made changes that were both painful and necessary.

Digit versions 1, 2, and 3 [left to right] show the evolution of the robot from a dynamic walking platform into a useful mobile manipulator. Agility

We had intended the next revision of Digit, Digit 4 EVT (Engineering Validation and Test), to be a relatively minor upgrade. But Agility’s new leadership insisted that the robot was missing key features that were essential if Digit was going to become a real product. So Digit 4 EVT instead incorporated a series of major changes in a highly compressed timeline, such as larger batteries and system-wide upgrades for safety and regulatory compliance, which added enough mass to dramatically alter the robot’s appearance and capabilities.

While early Digits were headless, Agility Robotics was able to justify a head for Digit 4 to optimize antenna and camera placement, and it turned out to be surprisingly useful for human-robot interaction.Christie Hemm Klok

I could only watch as others brought their own talents to bear to make Digit into a successful product, in gut-wrenching ways that didn’t always align with my vision. There were some especially difficult times when I felt like there were compromises made that didn’t seem necessary, but making those decisions was no longer my sole responsibility. I had to accept that Digit had grown far beyond me, and look for ways of influencing decisions rather than directing them. In the moment, it was incredibly frustrating, as Digit 4 EVT took a few steps backward from my vision of how humanoids should look and move.

Agility is in our name because agility is core to the future of the company. I want Digit to be lithe and graceful. When people see Digit, I want them to like the robot, to understand what it can do at a glance, and to feel that it’s there to help. But with Digit 4 EVT, all of that was sacrificed to functionality, because of course it had to be—the customer just needs the robot to do the work. The design process became a ruthless triage, with aesthetics and elegance of movement being delayed over and over again in favor of brutal functionality. For an engineer whose mind lives more in the future than in the present, it has been hard for me to accept this trajectory. And yet, through Digit 4 EVT’s commercial deployments, we began to really understand specific applications and what they required. We mapped the first 10 use cases Digit would perform, and then began designing Digit 5 from scratch based on everything we had learned.

Digit 5 will be Agility’s first real step toward a general-purpose robot. It marks our transition from imagining what a future humanoid robot should be to designing a product around the realities of customer deployments. These realities include things like European CE regulatory compliance, North American UL electrical-safety certifications, and Federal Communications Commission limits for electromagnetic radiation—all of which felt tangential to my dream for Digit, but were absolute requirements.

Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers while working 20 hours a day and lifting more than a human can.Christie Hemm Klok

Customer requirements helped us realize that safety in particular was one of the most critical barriers to scaling. In Digit 4’s commercial deployments, the robots had to work behind physical barriers, separated from humans at all times, to meet insurance and regulatory demands. This seemed silly to me, because I’ve never felt that our robots were dangerous, but we have to prove that they’re safe. And since keeping the robots in safety cages severely limited their usefulness, enabling Digit 5 to operate safely around people became a primary design goal. We spent two years on this challenge.

Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers. It will rely on an array of sensors to locate nearby people in a manner that’s certifiably safe, and then take actions based on that information. As a person approaches, Digit 5 is programmed to stop what it’s doing, set down its payload, sit on the floor, and cut power to its motors before the person gets close enough to touch the robot. This conservative approach reduces the risk to nearby people in a verifiable way, and we believe it’s the only approach that makes sense as a first step toward working alongside humans.

Yet this strategy also feels like a massive slowdown on the path toward robots becoming part of everyday life. Enabling coexistence with humans has influenced almost every aspect of Digit 5’s design: the shape of the legs and the body, the safety-rated sensors within protective housings, the isolated computers dedicated to safety, and more. All of these features increase the robot’s complexity, power consumption, mass, and physical size.

Digit 5 is Agility’s largest, heaviest, strongest, and most capable humanoid robot worker.

The robot’s design was driven by safety, with integrated protection for the robot and for the humans it will work around.Agility Robotics

Weighing over 120 kg, Digit 5 is a huge robot. It needed to achieve the lifting limits recommended under the U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health guidelines for human workers, which include repeatedly lifting 23-kg bins and reaching shelves 1.75 meters high. Digit is designed to perform tasks like these for 20 hours a day—something no human can do. This requires motors with enough power and torque to lift the load, but also enough precision to delicately control the force Digit applies when it makes contact with the world. To power those motors, we needed a large battery and a dock for rapid autonomous charging. The dock will deliver 240 amperes at 48 volts, which is enough current to make its thick charging cables visibly wiggle under the induced magnetic forces, while powerful fans blow air through cooling channels in the robot’s torso to keep the battery from overheating. The battery and cooling system takes up about 75 percent of Digit’s torso, but it will allow the robot to operate for 90 minutes and fully recharge during a 9-minute break, enabling near-continuous work.

All of this extra bulk means that Digit 5 can no longer run or jump the way previous generations could, and the svelte form I imagined has become physically impossible. In some ways, Digit 5 feels more like a forklift than the graceful humanoid I set out to build. But looking at the situation rationally, I believe this trade-off is necessary for any company that claims its humanoid can do this kind of work today: If you see a robot that looks like a human working in a factory or warehouse, it either can’t lift the required weight or can’t make it through the whole shift. And if it’s not covered with sensors, it’s likely not safe to stand next to.

The most visible change with Digit 5 is that humanlike legs replace the ostrichlike legs of our earlier versions. While the “backward” leg configuration was optimized for walking and running, we discovered that it created problems with squatting because the ankle will strike the ground. Digit 5 will spend a lot of time lifting heavy objects from near the floor, so we used a humanoid leg configuration with knee and hip motors that both contribute torque to help the robot stand up again.

When Digit detects an approaching human, the robot will lower itself to the floor and cut power to its motors. Agility believes this is the only near-term approach to verifiably reduce risk when the robot is working near people.Agility Robotics

Other companies building humanoid robots have copied the human form without ever understanding its purpose. It’s very frustrating that, to an outside observer, it now looks like we discarded Agility’s distinctive leg design and simply did what everyone else was doing. Yet I know that we arrived at this shape based purely on functional engineering choices. Making a robot look like a human is the easy part—without the function to match, and the understanding of the physics underlying that function, the whole point of the human form may be lost.

With the power, battery life, and safety features that we are designing into Digit 5, we will have a truly useful robot. But it also compromises on some things that are core to my vision and mission. I understand why we made the choices we did and can justify them all, but together they leave me unsatisfied. It’s the curse of the engineer.

I believe Digit 5 will be the scaling moment for Agility Robotics, the inflection point where we can begin deploying robots in large numbers. While the robot will continue carrying bins, our road map includes many more tasks, from picking individual items and tending machines, to preparing parts for assembly and shipping, and eventually doing assembly work itself. Its interchangeable tool interfaces and modular design will enable us to gradually upgrade its subsystems. It will be a platform for improvement, a source of data for future behavior training, and a viable product all at the same time.

Hurst stands between the previous version of Digit, Digit 4 [left], and Digit 5.Christie Hemm Klok

But I cannot love Digit 5. It’s the largest, heaviest, most expensive robot Agility will ever build, full of design compromises that enable it to be exactly the robot it needs to be right now rather than the robot I dreamed of. In the beginning, I envisioned steady progress on agility and dexterity, with each version becoming more dynamically capable. Instead, developing Digit 5 has required large detours to incorporate requirements that seemed unrelated to my original vision. However, I now recognize that tackling these challenges was always necessary. Customers and product requirements didn’t ruin my vision; they revealed what my vision was missing. This is how robots will achieve commercial success and make a real-world impact, which will bring me closer to my scientific dream as well.

We won’t have a humanoid that matches the capabilities of humans until it achieves that mastery of motion that inspired me to found Agility over a decade ago. I saw glimmers of it with the spring-mass locomotion of ATRIAS, and more glimmers with Cassie’s running gait.

I know that such mastery is physically possible with the tools and hardware that we have right now, and despite all of its compromises, Digit 5 will give us a practical foundation for pursuing that dream. I want every future version of Digit to be lighter and more graceful, to interact more naturally with humans, and to be better at manipulating objects and moving through the world, enabling robots to enter aspects of our lives that they haven’t been able to help with before. By the time I’m old enough to need assistance at home, I expect Digit will be up to the task.

With Digit 5, Agility has built a robot that will be useful in our world. Now I’m getting back to work to make it beautiful, too.

This article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

Jonathan W. Hurst is the co-founder and chief robot officer of Agility Robotics and a robotics professor at Oregon State University.

This is the most honest account I've read from a robotics founder. While Tesla and Figure are still showing demos, Agility has actually deployed robots in real customer environments, moved over 100,000 totes at GXO, and hit 98% accuracy at Schaeffler. Digit 5's specs are driven entirely by what customers need: 20 hours of work per day, 9-minute charge, 23 kg lift to 1.75 m shelves. That's real engineering for real problems. The tension between engineering vision and commercial reality is something every robotics founder will face. Professor Hurst lays it out without spin.

Why humanoid though? In particular, why bi-pedal? Why use legs at all? Are wheels surely better and easier? Legs seem like unnecessary complexity. Wheels on 'legs" for suspension can be a great alternative. I don't understand the obsession with humanoid form?

It seems to me that even at scale production, the robot we employ in industry should do jobs people cannot. Highly radioactive, highly toxic, and factors where the atmosphere needs to be unsuitable for humans. i.e., oxygen-deprived environment or low pressure/vacuum. Or use them on the 3rd shift when people are less willing to work.

Robots should increase manufacturing that was impossible to do in the past. We should be exploring new types of manufacturing, not replacing people in manufacturing that humans can do. That's how you create growth.

#3347. 10 Google Privacy Hacks Everyone Should Know

Your Gmail account doesn't just have one email address. In fact, it has unlimited addresses, but you need a hack to utilize them. When you're signing up for a new service, you can add another word to your email address, as well as the "+" symbol, to create an alias. For example, if your email is "[email protected]," and you're signing up for an Amazon account, you can use "[email protected]" as your email address. The email will still end up in your main inbox, as if you simply used [email protected]. Not only can this trick turn one Gmail address into an unlimited number of addresses, but it also helps you identify who sold your email address to spammers, because those emails will have the alias in the "To" field.

Gmail's web view has a crucial security feature that lets you view session logs. This feature is inexplicably buried at the bottom of the inbox, and the font size is tiny, so it's easy to miss. To find it, log in to Gmail on the web, and scroll to the bottom of your inbox. Click the Details button in the bottom-right corner, below "Last account activity." This will show you a pop-up that lists the devices, apps, and locations you've recently logged in from. This makes it easy to see if there's been any suspicious activity in your Google account, and you can click the Security Checkup link in the pop-up to review this data. Just note that if you use a VPN or a service like iCloud Private Relay, you might not recognize your own device's location. To check if unwanted apps have access to your Google account, you can visit this settings page.

Google wants to show you personalized search results, which initially feels very helpful, but it also ends up trapping you in an algorithmic bubble. The best way to break out of your search bubble is to periodically use other search engines, but if you wish to stick to Google, you can disable personalized search recommendations in Google Search and the Play Store on Android. Go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized Recommendations and Play Personalization.

Google tracks your web and app activity by default, which includes your search history, voice data (if you use the speak-to-search feature), and activity from sites, apps, and devices that use Google services. However, associated information, such as your location data, is also saved to your Google profile, which you might not assume gets included in "Web & app activity." Fortunately, you can disable this tracking by going to this settings page, scrolling down to "Web & App Activity," and turning off all options in this section.

Google's Timeline feature saves your location in Google Maps to create a map of places you've visited. This is useful if you want to keep track of your recent stops; however, Google can use Timeline data to help businesses see how effective their ads were, or how likely you are to visit nearby stores. Its confirmation page confirms this: "Depending on your settings, activity saved as history in your Google Account, including ad interactions, may also be connected to Timeline data to help nearby businesses estimate the likelihood that people will visit their stores. No personal information is shared with businesses."

Timeline isn't enabled by default, but in case you enabled it a while ago, and are no longer using it, you can turn it off by going to this settings page. Click Turn off, and delete your activity to remove Timeline data from your Google account.

You can't fully escape Google's ads or tracking, but you can disable personalized ads to stop the company from using your account data to show ads. To do this, go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized ads.

While Google claims that it isn't using your emails to train AI, the company does offer AI features that make your emails feel more robotic than human. One of these is "Smart Reply," which offers email reply suggestions such as "Got it. See you soon." I can type that on my own, and I feel uncomfortable with Gmail analyzing the contents of my emails and replies to offer suggestions that I wouldn't use anyway. You can disable this by going to Gmail Settings > General, or by visiting this settings page. Scroll down to "Smart features," and turn off the checkbox next to it. This will disable Smart Compose, Smart Reply, suggestions for pending replies and follow-ups, spelling, grammar, and autocorrect.

A physical security key is a great security upgrade. It's a physical barrier that prevents most ways to hack into your account remotely. Even if someone discovers your email ID and password, and has access to your two-factor authentication code, they won't get in without physical access to that key. You can check out Google's support page for physical security keys for more information on compatibility and setting up your security keys.

Google uses data from Gmail and Google Drive to target ads, which means that your emails, files, and photos could be used for monetization. To stop this, you'll need to disable Personal Intelligence. To turn it off, visit this settings page, and click Turn off Personal Intelligence.

#3346. Apple to investigate accident that killed three workers at iPhone parts factory in India

Reuters reports that three contract workers died after inhaling gas during an inspection at a Tata Electronics factory that produces iPhone components in India. Here are the details.

As frequent 9to5Mac readers probably know, Apple’s supply chain in India relies heavily on Tata, which manufactures iPhone components and accounts for a significant share of the country’s iPhone assembly operations.

Since Apple began diversifying its manufacturing operations away from China, India has emerged as a major production hub, with roughly a quarter of the world’s iPhones now manufactured in the country.

Earlier this year, Apple found itself linked to an environmental controversy in India, after the Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board investigated allegations that wastewater from a Tata facility had contaminated nearby farmland water.

A few weeks later, however, Tata said the regulator had dropped further action against the facility after the company addressed the concerns raised.

At the time, Tata said it had ordered separate testing related to the facility and that the results supported its position that the plant was operating within the rules.

However, the matter was apparently not fully resolved, as just three days later, Reuters reported that local health officials were still investigating complaints from nearby farmers.

And while there had been no major developments reported about the wastewater investigation since then, Reuters reported today that three contract workers died in an accident at the same Tata facility.

The three contract workers died during maintenance work on an effluent treatment ​plant operated by Nalco Water at the Tata facility, which is located in Hosur in Tamil Nadu, ​district official Dinesh Kumar said, adding that the deaths occurred when the workers inhaled gas while inspecting an external nano-filtration tank.

Reuters added that “Apple’s team is visiting ​the plant to assist in ​the ongoing investigation,” though the company did not respond when reached for comment.

The report added that Tata and Tamil Nadu authorities are also investigating the fatal accident, and noted that “production was not affected as the facility was closed for the Hindu festival of Deepavali this week.”

To read Reuters’ full report, follow this link.

#3345. I tested Lenovo's Yoga 9n 2-in-1 against the MacBook Pro for two weeks — impressive OLED and AI smarts cannot make up for poor gaming and weaker raw power

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

The Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 impressed me with its beautiful OLED touchscreen, versatile design and local AI performance. However, its high price, disappointing gaming performance and weaker raw processing power make it difficult to recommend over a MacBook Pro. It's a promising showcase for Nvidia's RTX Spark platform, but not quite the MacBook replacement I hoped for.

Beautiful design with versatile 2-in-1 functionality

Bright, vibrant OLED touchscreen with included pen

Impressive local AI performance thanks to CUDA cores

Smooth everyday productivity and multitasking

Raw creative performance trails high-end MacBooks

Gaming performance isn't great for the price

Battery life falls short of MacBook standards

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

You've probably heard the term "MacBook killer," especially following the launch of Nvidia's first RTX Spark laptops. Now, Apple has raised the stakes with its latest MacBook Pro models featuring the PROLED XDR Displays, and I wanted to see how these new machines actually stack up.

So, I put my 16-inch MacBook Pro M3 Max away for two weeks and used the Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 as my only laptop. I wanted to find out whether Nvidia's new platform could replace an older MacBook Pro, how it compares with Apple's latest flagships, and what makes RTX Spark laptops worth considering.

The Yoga makes a strong impression. Its versatile design, vibrant OLED touchscreen, and support for local AI workloads give me plenty to like. But after two weeks, I found that while it's a capable everyday laptop, its high price and performance trade-offs make it a more specialized alternative to a MacBook rather than a true replacement.

Nvidia  RTX Spark N1X with 5120-core GPU and 18-core CPU

Nvidia RTX Spark N1X 6144 Core GPU, 20-Core NPU

Nvidia RTX Spark N1X 6144 Core Blackwell GPU

2x USB-A, 2x USB-C, 1x HDMI 2.1, 1x 3.5mm Headphone jack, 1x SD card slot

2x USB-A, 2x USB-C, 1x HDMI 2.1, 1x 3.5mm Headphone jack, 1x SD card slot

This Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 is a versatile machine. It features a 360-degree hinge for tablet use, pen support, and a striking design with speaker grilles flanking the screen and keyboard.

Tent mode is perfect for sitting on my sofa and streaming episodes of “King of the Hill.” Folding the screen flat lets me use the giant 16-inch display as a primary monitor in the lab at work with an external keyboard and mouse.

Of course, holding a 16-inch screen like a tablet can feel a bit unwieldy. However, the ability to use the included pen in photo-editing apps like Photoshop is a nice feature. I also give Lenovo credit for including a pen in the box. There's even a small cradle that magnetically attaches to the top of the laptop, so you don't have to worry about losing the stylus.

The Yoga’s “Ice Blue" finish and polished accents also give this laptop a glamorous look, making it feel like a jewel on my desk. My Space Black MacBook just looks plain and boring compared to this Yoga 9n.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The keyboard and touchpad are also excellent. The dedicated number pad makes spreadsheet work far easier than on my MacBook, while the haptic touchpad matches Apple's gold standard. Clicks feel crisp, and special Windows-specific feedback for actions like closing windows and completing file transfers adds a nice tactile touch that my Mac lacks.

You can even use the pen on the haptic touchpad instead of writing directly on the screen. It can feel a bit strange, but it's another example of the flexibility this design offers. I could never imagine Apple doing that on a Mac.

Connectivity is another area where the Yoga has an advantage over my MacBook. In addition to HDMI and a full-size SD card reader, Lenovo includes two USB-A ports, which you won't find on a modern MacBook Pro.

Given the laptop's relatively thick 0.69-inch chassis and 4.28-pound weight, there's plenty of room for extra connections. During my two weeks with the Yoga, I left my dongles at home, which was a surprisingly refreshing change.

One of the biggest reasons I enjoy using the Yoga 9n 2-in-1 is the 16-inch OLED touchscreen. It's large, colorful, and bright enough to make everything from productivity work to streaming video enjoyable.

However, there's a new challenger in town. Apple's latest MacBook Pro, with its PROLED XDR display, has raised the bar for what we expect from a laptop screen. Although the numbers show that the Yoga 9n 2-in-1 doesn't quite match Apple's latest MacBook, that doesn't make it any less good.

Its 16-inch size gives me plenty of room to multitask with Google Chrome tabs and Slack while working in the lab. Brightness also reaches just over 1,000 nits in HDR, and one of my favorite shows, "King of the Hill," looks incredibly vibrant.

The episode where Bobby dresses up as the local college's mascot to help out Connie was a particularly good showcase. The oranges and other rich colors in the mascot suit practically jumped off the screen, making the animation look wonderfully alive.

In our lab tests, the Yoga's panel delivered a particularly high and oversaturated color volume, measuring 193.1% sRGB and 136.6% DCI-P3. It also ranked third in SDR brightness among the MacBook Pro 16-inch with M5 Max, Galaxy Book 6 Ultra, and HP Omnibook Ultra 16, reaching 449.8 nits and delivering an impressive 1,002 nits in HDR. Its 0.30 Delta-E result also placed it fourth in color accuracy among the laptops we compared.

However, the MacBook Pro 16-inch M5 Max PROLED XDR still comes out ahead in several important areas. It ranks first in brightness, reaching 549 nits in SDR and an impressive 1,949 nits in HDR. It also delivers the best color accuracy with a near-perfect 0.19 Delta-E.

However, Yoga is a more compelling matchup against my MacBook Pro M3 Max. As shown in the photo above, Lenovo's display produced particularly striking colors in the individual feathers of a parrot. Still, Apple's OLED display delivered more natural-looking detail and contrast, which I ultimately preferred.

Apple has also introduced touchscreen support on its new MacBook Pro and macOS, giving the Yoga serious competition in this category. If you're simply looking for the best touchscreen OLED laptop, Apple's latest MacBook Pro is hard to beat. However, choosing the MacBook means giving up the Yoga's 2-in-1 versatility and included pen.

Considering that the two laptops cost roughly the same in the configurations I tested, your choice will largely come down to pen support and whether you prefer Apple's ecosystem or Lenovo's more flexible design.

RTX Spark-powered laptops like this one aren’t really mainstream. They are more specialized notebooks focused on running local AI and taking advantage of native CUDA cores and the unified memory setup in this new chip from Nvidia. This makes them more of a laptop for developers and those who might want to run local agent platforms.

I tested this myself by downloading LM Studio and loading the Qwen 3.8-27b model. I took the Yoga 9n 2-in-1 offline and asked the model to write a 30-chapter novel about an earthquake in NYC and to describe the government falling apart and the city descending into chaos. The model produced an answer in 6 minutes and 20 seconds.

My final project for a college creative writing class was similar, so I was especially interested in seeing what the local model could produce. The chapters were relatively short and didn't include nearly as much detail as my own writing, yet the model still produced a coherent story. I was impressed by how much it could accomplish entirely on the laptop without an internet connection.

Out of curiosity, I also ran UL Procyon’s Text Gen benchmark. Across all the workloads, it scored 2,635, 2,346, 2,274, and 2,148. This was with the Phi-3.5-mini, Mistral 7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Llama-2-13B LLM instruct models using CUDA acceleration.

We don’t run these tests on every Windows laptop and Mac, so I have no reference to compare them to, but those numbers look great. According to UL’s own scoring page, scores are in the lower 200s for Intel Core Ultra chips and in the 1,000s for Snapdragon X2 Elite chips. This shows that this first-gen ARM chip from Nvidia is in a great place for AI performance.

For now, the most compelling reason to buy an RTX Spark laptop is its ability to run local AI workloads. That's a much more specialized use case than everyday productivity or gaming, and it's something worth considering before spending this much on a laptop.

The Yoga 9n 2-in-1 isn't designed to be a conventional productivity laptop. Nvidia's RTX Spark platform places a strong emphasis on AI, but that doesn't mean you can't use it for everyday work, creative applications, or even gaming.

For my typical laptop workload, the Yoga is more than capable. I regularly juggle Chrome tabs, Slack, and other applications while working in the lab, and I have no major issues keeping everything running smoothly. Photoshop works well for photo editing, and I have no trouble using Wondershare Filmora on Windows 11.

In other words, for everyday tasks, the Yoga 9n 2-in-1 was a perfectly capable replacement for my MacBook. The raw performance benchmark results, however, tell a different story and are a downside of this laptop.

For raw processing power, the Yoga 9n 2-in-1 struggles to justify its premium price. I give Nvidia credit for delivering competitive performance from its first-generation Arm chip. However, there's still a noticeable gap in demanding creative applications.

The MacBook Pro 16-inch M5 Max PROLED XDR outperformed Lenovo’s laptop across our major productivity and creative benchmarks, with particularly large leads in Geekbench 6 and Premiere Pro.

The Yoga scored 13,437 in Photoshop and 85,779 in Premiere Pro. Apple's MacBook Pro was also considerably faster in both, completing the test in 7,75 minutes in Photoshop and 4,47 minutes in Premiere Pro.

Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 (RTX Spark, 64GB RAM)

MacBook Pro 16-inch M5 Max PROLED XDR (M5 Max, 128GB RAM)

HP OmniBook Ultra 16 (RTX Spark, 32GB RAM)

In Geekbench 6, the Yoga scored 3,076 single-core and 20,084 multi-core. That's ahead of the Samsung Galaxy Book 6 Ultra (2,852 and 16,655) and puts it almost neck and neck with the HP OmniBook Ultra 16, which has RTX Spark (3,165 / 20,056). However, the MacBook Pro M5 Max remains considerably ahead at 4,359 single-core and 30,327 multi-core.

The results are particularly interesting when comparing the Yoga against my older 16-inch MacBook Pro M3 Max. Apple's previous-generation high-end chip scored 3,162 in Geekbench 6 single-core and 21,250 in multi-core. While the Yoga comes surprisingly close, it still falls behind. Its HandBrake result of 2:00, however, comfortably beats my older MacBook's 2:37.

The takeaway is that Nvidia's first-generation RTX Spark platform delivers solid everyday performance and competitive results in certain creative workloads. However, the Yoga doesn't consistently outperform newer high-end, near-fully specced-out MacBooks, making it harder to justify spending $3,999 if raw processing power is your priority.

Gaming and Nvidia go hand in hand, and this Yoga can certainly run demanding games. However, RTX Spark isn't a ticket to high-end gaming performance. Developers need to optimize their games for the new Arm-based architecture, or the games won't run at all. That's why I found out that some games from our lab's catalog (like Red Dead Redemption 2) won’t run at all. Others, like Far Cry 6, also misbehaved and didn’t run properly.

I technically can't play Forza Horizon 6 on my MacBook, so the Yoga still has the edge for my gaming needs. I enjoyed playing it with extreme settings and ray tracing enabled, and it averaged 38 frames per second at 1080p. Increasing the resolution dropped it to 23 fps, though. That's playable, but hardly the kind of performance you’d expect from a $3,999 laptop.

Assassin’s Creed Shadows (Medium, 1080p, 1880p)

Cyberpunk 2077 (Ray Tracing Ulta, 1080p, 1880p)

The results are more mixed in other games. In Cyberpunk 2077, the Yoga managed 34.55 fps at 1080p with Ray Tracing Ultra enabled, putting it in the same general range as the other laptops we tested. At higher resolution, it actually outperforms the MacBook and Samsung, although the HP was slightly ahead. Assassin's Creed Shadows is less impressive, with the Yoga reaching just 25 fps at 1080p.

Our synthetic benchmarks tell a similar story. In 3DMark Wild Life Extreme, the Yoga scored 21,830, averaging 130.21 fps. That's slightly behind the HP OmniBook Ultra 16, which scored 22,978 and averaged 137 fps.

Compared to a MacBook, the Yoga can game, but these results put it closer to an RTX 5070 gaming laptop. It won’t be a compelling choice if gaming is your main priority. You can get a more capable gaming laptop for this kind of money.

The top reason I love my MacBook Pro is its battery life, since I only have to charge it at most three times a week. When I tried to replace my Mac with the Yoga 9n 2-in-1, I quickly learned that this system can’t match what my MacBook Pro delivers. Even lab results show that this Yoga is behind the competition.

I put the Yoga 9n 2-in-1 through my daily workflow and started the day fully charged. With the screen at a comfortable 33% brightness, I worked through spreadsheets in Google Sheets, talking to my coworkers on Slack, and taking the occasional Google Meet meeting. By the time 3:30 got around, the battery was down to 62%. That was more than enough for when I got home, but after two hours of watching YouTube videos and cartoons on Hulu, I got the recharge warning and had to plug the laptop into power.

In our lab tests, MacBook Pro 16-inch (M5 Max PROLED XDR) claims first place with a marathon runtime of 21:24, followed in second by the Samsung Galaxy Book 6 Ultra at a solid 15:11. The Lenovo Yoga 9i 2-in-1 takes third place with 12:20, leaving the HP OmniBook Ultra 16 (RTX Spark) in fourth at 10:52.

Lenovo’s RTX Spark 2-in-1 is ahead of HP’s, but the numbers don’t lie: the Yoga 9n isn’t the best for battery life.

Lenovo’s Yoga 9n 2-in-1 is an expensive proposition. As configured, our unit costs $3,999 directly from Lenovo. The same configuration is slightly cheaper at Best Buy for $3,749.99. If you want to save money, you can also pick up the entry-level model with the N1X 18-Core Processor, 32GB RAM, and a 512GB SSD for $3,199.99 from Lenovo or $3,099 from Best Buy.

Those prices are pretty wild, but the ongoing RAM crisis and the tough economy are what contribute to them. Apple’s MacBooks are around the same price and, frankly, arguably deliver better performance.

You can get a 16-inch MacBook Pro with the NanoTexture PROLED XDR display, M5 Pro chip, 24GB RAM, and a 1TB SSD for $3,549.99. That’s still cheaper than the Yoga 9n 2-in-1. If you remove the nano-texture display, you can also upgrade to an M5 Max chip with an 18-core CPU, a 32-core GPU, 36GB RAM, and 2TB of storage for $4,799.99. That’s about $800 more than the Yoga, but you’d get more storage and a better screen.

The point is that these RTX Spark machines are not cheap. Most people shouldn’t consider buying them, since their use case is more specialized for AI than anything else. You can take that money and put it toward a brand-new MacBook Pro instead. Or, if you’re really on a budget, invest that $3,999 in a better Windows laptop like the Samsung Galaxy Book 6 Ultra, known for its OLED screen and battery life.

The Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 is an intriguing, beautifully built hybrid that serves as an impressive canvas for Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform. Thanks to a stunning 16-inch OLED touchscreen, included stylus, versatile 360-degree hinge, and local AI power, there is plenty to like. During my two weeks with it, the Yoga easily replaced my MacBook Pro for everyday productivity tasks like web browsing, Slack, and multimedia consumption.

However, at $3,999 as tested, it doesn't quite earn the title of "MacBook Killer." For heavy creative professionals, it might not be a strong enough MacBook replacement, given its weaker raw processing power in demanding benchmarks and rendering tasks. Likewise, due to its poor battery life, it simply didn't fit into my lifestyle the way my long-lasting Mac does.

If your daily workflow hinges on running local AI models on a flexible 2-in-1 canvas, the Yoga 9n will be for you. But for most power users seeking maximum performance and all-day endurance, a high-end MacBook Pro remains the smarter investment.

#3343. Garmin Cyclists Can Now Make Themselves Appear on Waze in Real Time

Cyclists who ride with Garmin gear can now appear as live, moving icons on the Waze driving app, and nearby drivers will receive an alert to slow down and watch for them on the road.

For riders already using Garmin devices, opting in costs nothing and adds a new layer of safety, particularly on roads where drivers may not expect cyclists. The feature is rolling out now, but you should be aware of its limitations.

Riders can simply opt in once through Garmin Connect. After that, sharing starts automatically when an outdoor cycling activity begins and stops when the ride ends. While a ride is underway, Waze users near the cyclist see a cyclist icon move along the road and receive a Live Cycling Alert reminding them to slow down and stay aware.

The feature runs on LiveTrack, Garmin's existing live location-sharing tool, which lets friends and family follow a rider's real-time location, speed, course, and more. Garmin says this collaboration extends that peace of mind to motorists, giving them greater awareness of their surroundings.

Garmin notes its location sharing is temporary and session-based. The rider's name, identity, and route are hidden, and no personal information is shared or displayed in Waze. Drivers see only an anonymous icon and the alert.

You'll need a few things to get this feature up and running:

A compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin watch

A phone running Garmin Connect with a data connection

An outdoor cycling activity (the feature doesn't apply to indoor rides)

The good news is using the feature is free: LiveTrack costs nothing on compatible Garmin bike computers and watches, and Waze is free for drivers.

This new feature is a great safety perk, but there are real-world caveats worth considering:

This feature is for Waze only. Alerts reach drivers only when Waze is open on their phone. Google Maps, which has far more users, is excluded, so a large portion of the drivers you share the road with won't see you this way.

It depends on your phone's signal. Your position travels from the Garmin to your phone, then to Garmin's servers, then to Waze, and finally to the driver's phone. On a patchy rural signal, a few seconds of lag could put the icon on the wrong side of a bend from where you actually are. A rider who leaves their phone at home or whose phone loses signal simply won't show up on a Waze map, as a ride without a data connection is invisible to Waze.

Finally, remember to treat this safety feature as an extra perk, not a guarantee. At the end of the day, it isn't a replacement for bike lights, bright clothing, and defensive riding.

#3342. IEEE Report Highlights How Members Are Engineering for Public Good

They include humanitarian initiatives and STEM education programs

Kathy Pretz is the editor in chief of The Institute, IEEE's member publication

IEEE MOVE, EPICS in IEEE, the IEEE Global Museum, and the TryEngineering Summer Institute, were some of the projects showcased in the 2025 Social Impact Report.

Advancing technology for the benefit of humanity isn’t just the tagline for IEEE’s mission as a public charity. It’s something that the organization’s more than 500,000 members strive to do all the time. IEEE’s recently released 2025 Social Impact Report showcases a variety of programs volunteers worked on to increase public awareness of technology’s impact on society, many of which The Institute covered.

Here is a selection of the programs from the report, with links to our related articles:

“The IEEE global community of more than 500,000 members and volunteers demonstrates what is possible when expertise is mobilized for the public good,” Sophia Muirhead, IEEE executive director and chief operating officer, said in a news release about the Social Impact Report. “Technology has the power to expand opportunity, strengthen communities and improve lives, and IEEE’s mission is to ensure that this power is used responsibly, ethically, and in service of humanity. The 2025 report shows how IEEE members and volunteers are advancing solutions that make a real difference in people’s lives around the world.”

Engagement research shows that members increasingly cited “giving back to my profession and the world community” as a reason for joining IEEE and renewing their membership, IEEE President Mary Ellen Randall said in her September column about the report.

“Humanitarian programs are not only meaningful,” she wrote. “They also are magnetic. They attract younger engineers, keep them engaged, and help them build a professional identity rooted in purpose and impact.

“IEEE has the opportunity to become the world’s leading convening force for developing interdisciplinary technology solutions to solve humanity’s most important challenges. Our future relevance will be defined not only by the technologies we advance but also by the problems we choose to help solve.”

Kathy Pretz is editor in chief for The Institute, which covers all aspects of IEEE, its members, and the technology they're involved in. She has a bachelor's degree in applied communication from Rider University, in Lawrenceville, N.J., and holds a master's degree in corporate and public communication from Monmouth University, in West Long Branch, N.J.
