#3313. From Chip Lab to Center Stage

This integrated circuit designer explains wearables to consumers

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute.

IEEE Member Preethi Ashwath is one of the few women who work in analog integrated circuit design, where about 11 percent are female.

Many engineers are more comfortable working behind the scenes developing technology than speaking to consumers about products. But Preethi Ashwath has learned to take center stage, talking about the “hearable” and wearable devices she has had a hand in developing as an analog integrated circuit designer in the consumer electronics division at Analog Devices of Wilmington, Mass.

The IEEE member is one of the few women who work in the specialized field, where about 11 percent are female, according to career platform Zippia.

Preethi Ashwath Employer Analog Devices, in BostonTitle Integrated circuit designerMember grade MemberAlma maters SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

Ashwath stepped out from behind the scenes last year to meet with attendees at the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas. She demonstrated Analog’s new earbuds, which track people’s heart and lung health through vibrations in their ear canals.

After she demonstrated her ability to explain the technology to consumers in simple terms, Analog selected her to represent the company at other events. She says she has “come to see speaking as part of contributing to the field, rather than something separate from technical work.”

She also gives technical talks on various aspects of electrostatic discharge (ESD) and other topics, as well as participates in panel discussions, she says, because they “reach engineers well beyond my immediate team.”

Ashwath is an active volunteer with the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society.

“Whether through designing semiconductor products, publishing technical articles, reviewing conference papers, or speaking at industry events, I try to contribute to the growth of the engineering community and the advancement of the field,” she says.

Ashwath, who grew up in Bengaluru, India, learned about electronics engineering from her high school physics tutor.

That introduction led her to take electronics as one of her core courses in her final years there. At the time, Ashwath’s older sister was pursuing an engineering degree.

“Between my interest in electronics and seeing her already on that path, it became clear to me that engineering was the way to go,” Ashwath says.

After earning a bachelor’s degree in electronics and communications engineering at the SJB Institute of Technology, in Bengaluru, she wanted to pursue a career in very-large-scale integration. But that changed once she moved to the United States and began her master’s program in electrical engineering at the University of California, Irvine.

She discovered her passion for circuits and devices during an internship at Intel in Santa Clara, Calif. She learned about circuit design, package design, and reliability verification tools such as Ansys Totem.

“Seeing every layer of the chip development process gave me a more complete picture of what goes into building a semiconductor product,” she says. “Through that experience, I realized I felt most connected to design.

“It was the hard work and creativity that drew me in. You start with a specification, build a circuit, simulate it, then wait for the chip to come back from fabrication. When your design works, it’s a real feeling of satisfaction. It teaches you patience and perseverance.”

After attaining her master’s degree, she was hired by Intel as an analog design engineer. She gained experience in mixed-signal circuit design before joining Analog. In her current role, she works on consumer hearables such as earbuds and wearables including fitness trackers and health monitors.

Her main focus is designing ESD pad rings, the borders of specialized circuits built around a microchip’s outermost edge to protect it from the discharge, which can damage circuit paths or introduce latent defects that lead to failures later in the chip’s life cycle.

“On a chip with multiple voltage domains, you have to plan how the protection structures are placed and connected across the whole pad ring—and get it right,” Ashwath says. “A mistake there could cause a chip to fail in the field in ways that are very hard to debug afterward.

“It’s detailed work that requires understanding both the device physics and how the whole chip fits together.”

Part of the job is designing and creating an integrated circuit’s building blocks, including ESD protection structures and other mixed-signal blocks. Ashwath conducts rigorous checks to verify they work as intended before being integrated into a chip.

She collaborates with ESD advisors, layout designers, and the digital team that designs the chip’s digital logic.

“I work with them to make sure my analog circuits and their digital blocks work together correctly,” she says. “No two days look exactly the same.”

In 2024 she was recognized with the company’s Impact Award for her “exceptional work on a critical project with significant cross-functional business impact.”

Ashwath was selected to represent Analog at events after a senior leader encouraged her to ask for high-visibility opportunities, she says.

“Most of my time is spent on designing circuits and simulations,” she says. “At CES, I stood in front of customers, engineers, and members of the press, explaining our technology and answering questions on the spot.”

The earbuds she demonstrated monitor minute vibrations from a user’s heart and lungs, according to the Analog website. The vibrations can detect arrhythmia, a leaky heart valve, or fluid in the lungs.

“Hearables are evolving from playing back audio to becoming health-monitoring platforms,” she says. “The ear turns out to be a good location for picking up physiological signals, so these devices can capture vital signs while someone is simply wearing them normally.

“The hard part is achieving high signal quality. The signals you’re trying to detect are very small and buried in the noise from the person’s movements and the surrounding environment.

“That’s where analog front-end design becomes critical. Extracting a meaningful signal from a noisy real-world environment is fundamentally an analog problem.”

Being face-to-face with customers at the conference was new to her.

“What struck me most was seeing how people react to the technology,” she says. “When you’re designing a block, you’re focused on specifications and margins. At CES, after explaining what the product does, I had a better understanding of why it matters to them.

“That connection between the circuit work and the final product is something you don’t always see from the design bench.”

Since the CES, Ashwath has presented other technologies she’s worked on. At the annual National Association of Music Merchants show in Anaheim, Calif., she demonstrated the A2B Automotive Audio Bus to the audio industry. The bus uses a low-cost unshielded twisted-pair cable to carry multichannel digital audio, control data, synchronized clock signals, and power in fewer than 50 microseconds, according to Analog.

“IEEE connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

At the company’s Global Technology Conference—an internal event held in Boston that draws engineers from the company’s more than 50 sites around the world—Ashwath led a demonstration of its solutions for augmented reality smart glasses.

“Each of these events has a different audience,” she says. “Learning to explain my technical work to different people has become a skill I’ve acquired.”

The most rewarding part of her job, she says, is seeing the end result of her work.

“You spend months on a design, and there’s a long wait between finishing it and finding out whether your instincts were right,” she says. “When the measurements match what you simulated, that’s the most satisfying moment in this job.

“The other part is knowing my work ends up in a real product. The circuits I design go into devices people actually use every day.”

Like many engineers, Ashwath joined IEEE to access research published in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. It keeps her current in a field that keeps moving, she says.

During her first year of membership, in 2021, she discovered other perks including networking and educational opportunities.

“IEEE connects you to a community outside your own company,” she says. “Attending lectures and technical talks exposes you to approaches and problems you wouldn’t encounter in your own work.”

She eventually began seeking out volunteer opportunities, specifically with IEEE conferences and journals, because they are “how you stay current with what’s happening in circuits and systems beyond your own day-to-day work,” she says.

“As an analog designer,” she says, “being connected to that broader community matters. The field moves, and you need a way to keep learning from it.”

She serves as a peer reviewer of papers for several IEEE conferences including the IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems and the IEEE International Midwest Symposium on Circuits and Systems. ISCAS is the flagship conference of the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society. MWSCAS is the oldest U.S. conference on the technologies.

“Someone has to assess whether submitted work is technically sound and worth presenting,” she says, “and that only happens if practicing engineers are willing to put in the time.”

The combination of learning from the community and contributing to it is what makes her membership worthwhile, she says.

“Analog design is a field where you’re always learning. Just when you feel you understand one architecture, there’s another one to learn,” she says. “Being an active learner isn’t optional in this field; it’s the requirement, and being part of the IEEE community helps with that.

“IEEE also connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry.

“Reviewing papers means reading what researchers are working on, which is often quite different from how the same problems get approached in a product environment. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

#3312. WhatsApp may soon replace the Communities tab on iOS

Some WhatsApp beta testers on iOS are seeing a new option in the app’s bottom navigation bar that replaces the Communities tab. Here are the details.

Over the past few years, WhatsApp has increasingly focused on Communities as more people have turned to messaging platforms to interact in smaller, more private groups rather than through traditional social networks.

At the same time, WhatsApp has been testing several features that make it easier for users to see which of their contacts are online and available to chat.

Back in May, WABetaInfo found that WhatsApp was developing a new Contacts hub that would bring together users’ favorite contacts, as well as those who were currently online or had recently been active.

A few weeks later, WhatsApp began testing a new green dot indicator on iOS to make it easier to identify contacts who were online.

Now, WABetaInfo reports that WhatsApp is rolling out the new Contacts hub to some iOS beta testers, replacing the Communities tab in the app’s bottom navigation bar.

The new tab includes a section with favorite contacts and a full contact list. Users can see their favorite contacts at the top of the screen, making it easier to start a conversation with them. They can also sort the full contact list by activity, alphabetical, and birthdays. With alphabetical, the app organizes contacts by name. With activity, WhatsApp shows who is currently online at the top of the list. WhatsApp marks these contacts with a green dot, so users can easily distinguish them from offline contacts. WhatsApp also sorts recently active contacts by last seen, so users can quickly identify who was active most recently. With birthdays, WhatsApp sorts contacts by their upcoming birthday, so users can see who has a birthday coming up soon.

The site notes that the new tab also allows users to add contacts directly, with the option to sync them to their iPhone’s address book.

As for Communities, the feature itself isn’t going away, but rather being moved to a dedicated filter in the Chats tab.

WABetaInfo also notes that WhatsApp is experimenting with potentially replacing the Updates tab, rather than Communities, with the Contacts tab in a future configuration.

For now, the new Contacts tab is available to a limited number of beta testers running the latest WhatsApp beta for iOS via TestFlight, with a broader rollout expected over the coming weeks.

To read WABetaInfo’s full report, follow this link.

#3310. HomeKit Weekly: SwitchBot’s Curtain Track 4 is the easiest smart curtain retrofit yet

The worst part of owning smart curtain motors is charging them, because it usually means taking the whole motor down from the track or running a really long USB cord to charge it. Today, SwitchBot has released the SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 aimed at solving that problem with a battery module that detaches on its own, so the motor stays in place, and you only take down the part that needs to charge.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

The SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 is a retrofit motor for curtains that hang on a U-rail track. You hang it on the track between the curtain hooks, run a one-tap calibration in the SwitchBot app, and your existing curtains can then be motorized and used in your smart home. There’s no drilling, no rewiring, and no need to position magnets to stick to the rail, as earlier SwitchBot curtain motors required. SwitchBot claims the whole setup takes about 30 seconds.

One thing to check first: this version is for U-rail tracks only, not curtain rods.

The Battery+ version pairs a small built-in battery with a detachable 5,000mAh module for a total of 6,400mAh. SwitchBot rates it at up to 12 months of use for each charge, depending on curtain weight and movement frequency. When it needs charging, you pull the module off, charge it via USB-C, and clip it back on. SwitchBot also sells a Solar version that uses a small panel to keep the battery topped off if the window gets enough sun.

The motor itself connects via Bluetooth, so getting it into Apple Home requires a compatible SwitchBot Hub, which brings it there via Matter. Once it’s there, the curtains work like any other window covering in your Home app. You can add them to scenes, control them with Siri, and include multiple windows in a single automation. It’s always nice to time smart curtains/shades with dusk/dawn as well.

SwitchBot’s built-in QuietDrift mode opens the curtains slowly in the morning, at about half a centimeter per second, so the room fills with daylight gradually rather than all at once. SwitchBot says it runs at around 25 dB in that mode. You can also give the curtain a gentle tug by hand and the motor takes over, which is great if you don’t have your iPhone with you or someone doesn’t have access to your Apple Home setup.

SwitchBot built it in a way to correct drift over time, so you shouldn’t need to recalibrate it if it gets off.

The SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 turns the U-rail curtains you already have into Apple Home window coverings without replacing anything. The detachable battery is the best feature here, as it lets you charge it without a long cord.

The SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 is available now on Amazon and directly from SwitchBot.

#3306. If you bought an iPhone Duo, have you kept or returned it? [Poll]

When Apple announced the iPhone Duo back in September, the company called it “the most transformational change to iPhone since the original,” and there’s no doubt that it generated a huge amount of excitement.

But a new report suggests that for some buyers the novelty quickly wore off, and they ended up returning their devices. Is this just a handful of people, or is it more common … ?

It’s been a very long time since any smartphone launch has generated quite so much buzz. Apple called it a breakthrough in iPhone design.

iPhone Duo features a breakthrough foldable design that’s beautiful, versatile, and durable, opening up possibilities that feel entirely new yet remarkably familiar […]

“iPhone Duo is the most transformational change to iPhone since the original. With an entirely new design and intuitive experiences, it shows what’s possible when hardware and software are engineered together and redefines what it means to use a foldable phone,” said John Ternus.

Despite not really being the target market for the phone, I was still wowed by the launch video and remained incredibly impressed when I got some hands-on time with one.

Many couldn’t resist buying one despite the price – but The Verge notes that not everyone has ending up keeping the device. Apple allows you to return any product within 14 days for a full refund without having to give any reason. That window has come to an end for some of the first buyers and the site’s Alison Johnson spoke with some of those who’d decided to take advantage of it.

The iPhone Duo replaced both my iPhone 15 Pro Max and my iPad Mini 6. It now is my phone and iPad mini in my pocket. This is the dream phone I never knew I wanted.

And for the lack of Face ID, Touch ID works perfect with my Apple Watch. And even without wearing it, I don’t see the big deal of the ‘huge’ effort of bringing my finger to a button.

For the lacking 5x zoom that I had on my Pro Max, I haven’t had a moment yet that I wanted to use it to be honest. Those moments will definitely arise, but the lack of that camera cannot go up against the amazing overall experience of the iPhone Duo.

But the more fundamental reason for some is that it hasn’t really lived up to their hopes for a multifunctional device.

“If I can have an iPad in my pocket, that would be great.” So thought Ben Seligson, a content creator, photographer, and now former iPhone Duo owner […] “Usually I’d throw a YouTube video on the iPad or throw a podcast up. And then I start cooking dinner and leave my iPad in one spot, but I’d have my phone in my pocket if I got a text, or I needed to set a timer or something like that.” With the Duo, the phone was also the iPad on the counter, so a quick reply became much more of an interruption.

I’m curious as to whether this is just a small minority of buyers or a more common phenomenon. If you bought a Duo early enough to have hit the end of the return window, please take our poll to let us know whether you decided to keep it or return it – and do share your reasons in the comments (which are now back).

Oh, and the good news for anyone buying one now is that you’ll have a lot longer to make up your mind, with the extended return window for the holidays in place. You can now return anything bought today through January 8.

Lightyears before Hollywood’s obsession with beauty biohacking, Keren Bartov was already using medical-grade, high-tech skin care tools to bring glow-from-within radiance to stars’ visages. Her results were most recently seen on clients Cate Blanchett, Elizabeth Debicki and Mikey Madison, who visited the celebrity facialist’s Notting Hill studio for bespoke facials ahead of the annual Harper’s Bazaar Women of the Year Awards in London on Nov. 5.

The 47-year-old aesthetician also saved A-listers from a cross-Atlantic trip by popping up in LA with her suite of skin-plumping, jawline-snatching devices and her own Keren Bartov Advanced Skin Care serums and creams ahead of the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show and Academy Museum Gala last month. VS Angels models Joan Smalls, Jasmine Tookes, Elsa Hosk and Amelia Gray beamed with Bartov’s signature glow at the lingerie company’s takeover of Sony Pictures Studios on Oct. 18, as did longtime clients Demi Moore and Mila Kunis at the star-studded Academy fundraiser. “Before a major event, my goal is for the skin to look its absolute best while remaining calm, balanced and refreshed. The last thing I want is to cause irritation or an unexpected reaction right before a red carpet,” notes Bartov. “I often combine technologies that help improve the appearance of firmness and texture with lymphatic drainage, gentle enzymatic exfoliation and skin care that delivers hydration and radiance.”

In fact, the U.K.-based skin expert has an arsenal of more than 50 technologies — in which she’s invested millions of dollars to ensure only the most state-of-the-art facials — “but the number itself isn’t what matters. I never introduce a technology or ingredient simply because it’s new or everyone is talking about it. For me, innovation has to be backed by science, safety and meaningful results.”

Her pre-event treatments are based on her 90-minute Signature Glow Facial ($500 to $900), available at her London and Tel Aviv clinics. She incorporates her namesake luxury skin-care products along with the Onda Pro (which uses microwave and cool waves to tighten, contour and reduce cellulite), the Lumenis TriLift (which incorporates radiofrequency, microneedling and muscle stimulation for firming and lifting), the buzzy XERF (Bartov was among the first to add the radiofrequency skin-tightening machine to her menu) and other non-invasive, multi-modality medical devices.

For the Victoria’s Secret and Academy events, “I treated clients with completely different skin concerns, which meant every protocol was different. What they all had in common was the desire for skin that looked naturally healthy, fresh, and radiant, creating the perfect canvas for makeup without ever looking overdone,” says Bartov.

A former aspiring actor, Bartov’s unexpected path to Hollywood began in southern Israel, where she opened a tiny skin clinic in her community before expanding to Tel Aviv. Fellow Israeli Gal Gadot became her first celebrity client and earliest cheerleader, and pushed Bartov to bring her methodology to London in 2023.

Bartov recently debuted a Festive Facial to prep clients’ faces for upcoming holiday soirees. Like her signature offering, the clinical treatment uses up to five tech tools in a specific sequence to address collagen loss, pigmentation, acne and signs of aging. Visitors can also pick up her limited-edition holiday gift sets (from $400) created in collaboration with British artist Clym Evernden, who also drew up a winter window dressing for Bartov’s Notting Hill clinic.

Can’t book a flight or secure an appointment at her overseas outposts? Bartov’s skin-care sets are also available online for anyone to achieve her red carpet-ready glow from home.

Ahead, Bartov shares what she can’t live without (including her most priceless essentials), the ingredients and devices that have piqued her interest and those that she recommends skipping.

In a nutshell, what led you to becoming a star-trusted skin expert?

Keren Bartov: Ever since I was a little girl, I’ve been drawn to everything related to beauty, aesthetics and skin care. It was always something I loved, but as I got older, I realized I also wanted a stable career, something I could build and grow over time, so I decided to study cosmetology. Very quickly, I discovered there was so much more to it than I had imagined. I fell in love with the field, started studying and exploring it in depth and realized I had found my place.

Today, I feel like I’ve somehow managed to bring all the worlds I love together: beauty, aesthetics, creativity, working with people and even a little bit of the entertainment world, especially when I’m preparing actresses and models for some of their biggest moments.

For more than 17 years, I’ve been studying, researching and exploring advanced technologies and treatment methods from around the world. What started as genuine curiosity and passion eventually became the treatment method I’ve developed over the years.

Developing my own skin-care line was a natural extension of that journey. I wanted to take the knowledge and experience I’d gained in the treatment room and translate it into products that could become part of my clients’ everyday routines. To this day, nothing excites me more than seeing how the right treatment and skin-care routine can transform not only someone’s skin, but also their confidence.

How do you decide what new product or technology makes the cut? What are the red flags that tell you something is just a fad?

I never introduce a technology or ingredient simply because it’s new or everyone is talking about it. For me, innovation has to be backed by science, safety and meaningful results.

Before incorporating a new device or product, I look at the research behind it, how it works, whether it’s suitable for different skin types and how it can complement the treatments and products I already use.

I take exactly the same approach when developing my own skin care. Every formula needs to have a clear purpose. For example, with Melanin Correcting Serum, the focus is on addressing the appearance of uneven pigmentation, while Hydra Reboost Cream is about providing the hydration and comfort the skin needs. They’re different products designed to address different concerns, and that’s exactly how I believe skin care should work.

What ingredients, devices, or innovations are exciting you most right now, and why?

One technology I’m particularly excited about is Onda Pro, which uses targeted microwave energy to address concerns including skin firmness and the appearance of facial contours. What interests me most is how I can incorporate it into a broader, personalized treatment protocol.

Another is XERF, a radiofrequency technology designed for non-invasive skin tightening. I was among the first practitioners in the world to work with it, and I love being involved in the early stages of exploring new technologies, understanding their capabilities and discovering who can truly benefit from them.

When it comes to ingredients, I’m a strong believer in peptides, active acids, and ingredients supported by solid clinical research. I’m not interested in whatever ingredient happens to be trending online. I’m interested in what can genuinely address a specific skin concern.

Peptides are particularly interesting to me, which is why I love incorporating a peptide serum into a targeted skin-care routine. I’m also a big believer in exfoliating acids when they’re used correctly. My Booster Peel & Glow Serum reflects that approach: using active ingredients with a clear purpose, rather than exfoliating simply for the sake of it.

To me, real innovation isn’t always about discovering something entirely new. It’s about finding smarter, more precise ways to use ingredients and technologies that have already proven themselves.

What beauty trends do you suggest clients skip?

I’m not a big fan of beauty gimmicks that look amazing on social media but don’t necessarily deliver meaningful, long-term results.

Sheet masks and under-eye patches are good examples. They can provide a temporary boost of hydration or make the skin feel refreshed, but I don’t see them as a substitute for skin care that genuinely works on the skin.

I’d much rather see someone invest in a well-formulated serum that addresses their actual skin concerns. That’s why I’ve always placed so much emphasis on active formulas, whether it’s Advanced Skin Serum as part of a consistent routine or Melanin Correcting Serum for someone looking to address uneven skin tone.

I’m also cautious about trends like at-home microneedling. It’s a procedure that requires professional knowledge, and when done incorrectly, it can cause irritation, infection and damage to the skin. Another trend I’m not a fan of is using active acids without understanding their concentrations, how they interact, or whether they’re suitable for your skin.

I absolutely believe in advanced skin care and using multiple products, but every product should have a purpose. I don’t believe in adding something to your routine just because it’s gone viral. For me, the question isn’t how good a product looks on camera. It’s what it actually does for your skin.

Walk us through your treatments. What do you consider when creating custom protocols for clients?

No two people have exactly the same skin, so no two treatments should ever be identical. I start with a thorough skin assessment, looking at texture, hydration levels, pigmentation, elasticity and sensitivity. I also consider age, lifestyle, skin-care habits, previous treatments and, of course, what the client wants to achieve.

One of the things that makes my method different is the ability to address several concerns within a single treatment. For example, I might combine technologies targeting firmness, texture, hydration, and radiance, carefully selecting devices that complement one another. But personalization doesn’t end when the client leaves the clinic. I also look at what they’re using at home, because professional treatments and daily skin care should support one another.

Someone dealing with pigmentation might benefit from incorporating Melanin Correcting Serum into their routine, while someone whose skin needs more hydration might be better suited to Hydra Reboost Cream. In other cases, I might focus on introducing active serums gradually or adjusting the evening routine.

I don’t believe in a one-size-fits-all facial or a one-size-fits-all skin-care routine. I believe in understanding exactly what the skin needs and building the right protocol around it.

What are your top tips for a solid foundational skin-care routine? What people avoid?

I’m a big believer in a comprehensive skin-care routine that incorporates multiple products and active ingredients, as long as they’re carefully selected and work well together. I don’t think we should be afraid of having several steps. What’s important is understanding what each product does and why it’s there.

For me, the foundation of great skin is proper cleansing, targeted active ingredients, hydration, and daily sun protection.

In the evening, I always recommend starting with a double cleanse. I use my Micellar Water to remove makeup and impurities, followed by a gentle milky cleanser to thoroughly cleanse the skin.

Once the skin is clean, I like to work with different serums depending on its needs. Booster Peel & Glow Serum is one of my favorites for improving the appearance of skin texture and radiance, while Advanced Skin Serum is an essential part of my own routine.

For clients dealing with uneven skin tone and pigmentation, I often recommend Melanin Correcting Serum. I also love incorporating a peptide serum, as peptides are among the ingredients I believe in for supporting firmer, healthier-looking skin.

I place enormous importance on nighttime skin care. While we sleep, the skin goes through natural renewal and repair processes, and I love using those hours to give it targeted care.

One ingredient I believe in most is retinol. It’s one of the most extensively researched ingredients in skin care, with well-established benefits for improving skin texture, the appearance of fine lines, and uneven skin tone over time.

That belief was also behind the development of Next Gen, my retinol-infused night cream. I consider it an important part of a targeted evening routine, with the frequency of use adjusted to the individual’s skin.

Hydration is equally important. I love Hydra Reboost Cream for keeping the skin feeling comfortable and moisturized, and Hydration Glow Spray is one of my favorite finishing touches for an instant boost of freshness and radiance. It’s also a product I love having with me when I travel.

In the morning, my focus is on hydration, protection and maintaining healthy-looking skin. Sunscreen is absolutely non-negotiable.

Of course, not every active ingredient is suitable for everyone, and I don’t recommend layering strong acids and retinol indiscriminately. It’s important to tailor combinations and frequency of use to the skin’s needs and tolerance.

What should we avoid? Constantly switching products, combining active ingredients without understanding how they work together and expecting overnight results.

I always compare skin care to going to the gym. If you want to see real results, you have to be consistent. It’s the combination of the right products, a consistent routine and professional treatments that makes the difference.

What are some essentials that you can’t live without right now?

If there’s one skin-care product I can’t live without, it’s my Advanced Skin Serum. It’s one of the products I reach for every single day and a true essential in my routine. I love how it helps my skin look smoother, fresher and more radiant. No matter where I’m traveling, it always comes with me.

I’m a big believer in movement and taking care of my body. Strength training is an important part of my routine, and I also love going for walks. With all the traveling and work, it’s my time to clear my head and focus on myself.

I love activewear that’s comfortable enough for a workout but stylish enough to wear outside the gym. Alo Yoga’s Airlift leggings are exactly my style, especially on days when I’m going straight from a workout to meetings or errands.

I absolutely love Victoria Beckham’s tailoring. There’s something so precise, feminine and effortlessly elegant about her designs. A beautifully tailored blazer and trousers are a combination I can always rely on, especially for meetings and events.

I love this bag. There’s something iconic and timeless about it, and I’ve always preferred pieces that never go out of style.

For me, great foundation should still let your skin look like skin. I love a lightweight base that evens out the complexion, adds freshness and lets the skin’s natural texture show through. That’s exactly the kind of makeup I gravitate toward.

I love makeup that adds a subtle touch of light without looking heavy. This is one of those products that can instantly bring a little color and radiance to the face, especially when I’m going straight from a long workday to dinner or an event.

I love candles and beautiful home fragrances, and Diptyque is one of my favorite brands. Baies has that elegant, comforting scent that instantly creates a lovely atmosphere at home. Lighting a candle at the end of the day is one of my little rituals.

And one thing I could never leave off the list: Evenings at Home With My Husband and Kids.

This might not be a product, but it’s the one thing I truly can’t live without. I spend so much time traveling and working around the world that the simplest moments at home mean the most to me. Family dinners, spending time with my kids or just having a quiet evening with my husband are the moments I look forward to most.

#3302. Build a Hidden Lock With a Magnetic Imager

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum.

Only a programmable secret gesture with a magnet can open this lockbox. (Or a hammer. It’s a proof of concept.)

Like many a nerd, I have a certain fascination with locks. This originates in reading the memoir Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman as a teenager, in which Richard Feynman recounts picking locks and cracking combinations while at his day job working on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos. I currently have a couple of locksport pick sets and training locks that I purchased at hacker conferences over the years (although I’m still terrible at it), and I delight in the YouTube exploits of folks like the LockPickingLawyer.

All of which left me wondering if I could try building an interesting lock. One dodge that lockmakers have long used to challenge would-be plunderers is to conceal the existence of the lock itself. A modern variant of this is the magnetic lock, where a magnet is held or slid against an innocuous portion of a door or box, releasing a catch. The problem with this is that, once you guess the location of the lock, any strong magnet will open it.

So I started thinking about embedding an RFID reader under the surface and resigning myself to keeping track of yet another access card. But then I stumbled across something much more interesting: SparkFun’s US $100 magnetic imaging tile. I realized I could use this to build a magnetic lock that opens with a programmable secret gesture.

I used a few discrete components to drive the servo motor and put the lock into program mode [top], controlled by a Teensy 4.1 microcontroller [middle]. An array of Hall-effect sensors detect magnetic fields [bottom].James Provost

The magnetic imaging tile is a small-run SparkFun board based on the work of Peter Jansen. It features an 8-by-8 grid of Hall-effect sensors, and uses an SPI interface to talk to the microcontroller of your choice. These sensors can detect both the magnitude and polarity of a magnetic field, and the board can report its measurements hundreds to thousands of times per second, depending on how much processing power your microcontroller has available. This is easily fast enough to capture the motion of a magnet being moved by hand across the board’s sensor area—my secret gesture.

An interesting thing about using magnetic fields is that if I was in extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting, something I couldn’t do with an RFID reader. The copper sheet would act as a Faraday cage, blocking any RFID signal, along with any other electromagnetic fields an attacker with an EMF meter might use to locate the lock.

I chose a Teensy 4.1 as my microcontroller. I like the Teensy because it offers loads of input/output, a 600-megahertz processor, a megabyte of RAM, and a built-in SD card, all in a slim package with an equally slim $32 price tag.

Wiring the Teensy to the magnetic-imaging tile was trivial, only complicated by the fact that one side of the board has a silk-screen error that misidentifies the SPI connections (SparkFun says this will be fixed in future runs of the board).

In extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting.

To create the gesture-recognition software, I once again turned to vibe coding. If you read my Hands On piece in the April 2026 issue of IEEE Spectrum on creating a teletext suite for ham radio, you’ll know I’ve been grappling with how vibe coding should be used in DIY projects, if at all. So this time, instead of letting Claude write all the software, I confined it to writing just two support libraries, which you can find in our online repository at https://github.com/IEEESpectrumHandsOn.

One library is in charge of recording a lock gesture and saving it to the Teensy’s nonvolatile storage. The other library monitors the tile and reports whether or not a newly detected gesture passes a selectable threshold to be considered a match.

I wrote the top-level code myself to keep it as DIY as possible. This code handles things like a button that puts the system in gesture-recording mode after a brief delay, the indicator LED for recording mode, and the code that operates the physical locking mechanism.

Hall-effect sensors rely on a current passing through a p-type slab of silicon. A magnetic field passing through the silicon deflects charge carriers toward the edges of the slab, creating a voltage proportional to the field [left]. By looking at the intensities of the voltages across an 8-by-8 grid of sensors, the microcontroller can reconstruct a gesture [right]. James Provost

Of course, I needed something to lock to demonstrate my proof of concept. I bought a wooden craft box and removed the existing lid latch. I glued a notched beam inside the lid and built a mechanism that uses a servo motor to rotate another beam in and out of this notch. I will be the first to admit this mechanism goes beyond “simple” and into “simplistic,” but it’s sufficiently robust for my demo. The box has ample room for the magnetic imaging tile to be mounted against one wall, along with the Teensy and other supporting electronics. These include a battery pack, the recording button, and a small additional board with two NPN transistors. These convert the Teensy’s 3.3-volt control signals to a 5-V signal needed to drive the servo.

Once it was all put together, I soon discovered that the small size of the magnetic tile’s sensing area—just 3 centimeters square—made it easy to fit the tile inside the box but hard to do the unlock gesture on the outside so that it is read correctly. Marking the outline of the sensor area on the outside defeated the point of having a hidden lock, so instead I once again turned to mining my Irish heritage. I created a Celtic knotwork pattern that runs in a band across the front of the lockbox (I used an online knotwork generator and then projected and traced the pattern onto the box). Using the pattern as a camouflaged reference grid I can make a repeatable gesture within the confines of the sensor area. (To make the gestures I’m using a magnetic stylus borrowed from a ferrite core-memory kit we featured in 2022.)

There’s obvious room for improvement in any more serious installation. The biggest drawback currently is that if the box is locked when the battery runs out, you can’t open it again without breaking something. This could be solved by adding a hidden inductive charging coil. Nonetheless, the demo lockbox works well—now I just have to think what I should store in it!

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum. He currently helms Spectrum's Hands On column, and is also responsible for interactive projects such as the Top Programming Languages app. He has a bachelor's degree in experimental physics from Trinity College Dublin.

#3301. All of These Nebula Projectors Are up to $700 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Black Friday is still a couple of weeks away, with the big shopping event falling on November 27, but Amazon's early Black Friday sale is already bringing some worthwhile discounts on Soundcore's Nebula projectors. Prices start at $299 for the compact Nebula P1i and go up to $2,799 for the premium X1S 4K laser projector, with savings of up to $700 across the models we've rounded up. There's quite a bit of variety here, too, from battery-powered projectors you can take camping or move between rooms to more powerful 4K models designed for a dedicated movie-night setup.

The Soundcore Nebula P1i is down to $299 from $399, while the Nebula P1 is $699.99, down from $799. Both offer 1080p resolution and Google TV, but their speaker setups are what make them interesting. The P1i has two 10W speakers that flip out and rotate to direct sound toward your seating area, while the P1's speakers detach completely and can run wirelessly for up to 20 hours. The P1 is also brighter at 650 ANSI lumens versus the P1i's 380, though you'll need a power outlet for either projector since neither has a built-in battery.

Small enough to slip into a bag, the Nebula Capsule 3 and Capsule 3 Laser are worth considering if you want something you can easily take on trips or move around the house. The standard Capsule 3 is down to $399 from $529, saving you $130, while the Laser version is $649.99, down from $749.99. Both offer 1080p resolution, automatic image adjustments, and up to 2.5 hours of battery life, although the Laser model is a little brighter at 300 ANSI lumens compared with the standard model's 200.

Taking movie night outdoors is a little easier with a battery-powered projector, and both the Nebula Mars 3 Air and Mars 3 are designed for just that. The smaller Mars 3 Air is down to $519.99 from $599.99, offering 1080p resolution, 400 ANSI lumens of brightness, and up to 2.5 hours of playback. The larger Mars 3, now $899.99 from $999.99, steps things up with 1,000 ANSI lumens, up to five hours of battery life in Eco mode, and a more powerful 40W speaker. It also has a weather-resistant design that's useful for camping or backyard screenings, though its extra bulk might make it less convenient to carry around.

If you're ready to move beyond 1080p, the Nebula Cosmos 4K SE at $1,099.99 (originally $1,299.99) offers a more affordable way to get 4K resolution. Its hybrid LED and laser light source delivers up to 1,800 ANSI lumens, while its Dolby Vision support helps bring out more detail in compatible movies and shows. You also get Google TV and automatic image adjustments for easier setup, though it doesn't have a built-in battery, so you'll need a power outlet nearby.

At the premium end of Nebula's lineup, the X1 and newer X1S are designed for a more serious home theater setup. The X1 is down to $2,299 from $2,999, saving you $700, while the X1S is $2,799 from $3,299. Both use triple-laser technology with 4K resolution, Dolby Vision, and optical zoom, but the X1S has a considerable advantage in brightness, reaching up to 6,000 ANSI lumens compared with the X1's 3,500. That extra brightness is useful in rooms with some ambient light, but the tradeoff is louder fan noise.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Use price tracking tools to determine if the deals you're keeping tabs on are actually a deal. If you feel like that's too much work, we already do that for you, so follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products makes you focus and make smarter decisions.

Not all Black Friday deals are as good as they might seem. Unfortunately, Amazon is known to manipulate prices to trick you, but there are tools at your disposal you can use to see if the deals are actually good or not. If that seems like too much work, you can just follow our Black Friday coverage (we're already doing all the searching and vetting for you). Some other tips are making sure you're not being sold an older or cheaper version, and to always read reviews.

#3300. iPhone is the winner of new battery test, topping all Androids

Last week CNET published an extensive battery test and the iPhone came out on top. But it wasn’t just one iPhone model that performed well, as several iPhones topped CNET’s list.

CNET pitted 32 modern smartphones against each other to see how battery life compared.

The winner? iPhone 18 Pro Max, which was followed closely by two other iPhone models.

Here’s the top 10 list, which contains several ties:

The 18 Pro Max has won the camera test, battery life test, and speed test over the top Android flagships. Other phones and Foldables might get more hype but when it comes time to perform head to head...the iPhone Pro Max comes out on top and we have video proof

As you can see, iPhone 17 and iPhone 18 Pro both tied for second place alongside a pair of Android models. iPhone 18 Pro Max was the sole model that beat every other.

Each battery test is going to be a bit different, so results may vary depending on how you stress-test a phone. That said, here’s the method behind CNET’s test:

Each phone was put through a 3-hour streaming video test and a 45-minute anecdotal stress test, both with the battery at 100%. The results show the remaining battery percentage – the higher, the better. We averaged the results to determine our rankings

CNET says that in the 45-minute stress test they “stream videos, make a video call, play games and scroll social media.” So it’s an attempt at replicating normal use.

What’s your takeaway from the battery test results? Let us know in the comments.

#3297. IEEE Xplore Digital Library Adds AI Assistant

The search tool offers summaries and verifiable source links

Claire Olini is the senior manager for IEEE Corporate and Strategic Product Launch and Engagement.

Michael Spada is director of IEEE Product Launch and Engagement Strategy.

IEEE recently released the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite, built on the full text of millions of peer-reviewed publications in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. The library offers full-text access to IEEE standards, journals, magazines, conference proceedings, and more.

Researchers who use the AI suite to search the digital library receive answers grounded in verified scientific results, ensuring a high level of accuracy and trust.

Powered by a proprietary AI system optimized for STEM literature, the suite introduces powerful, intelligent features within the digital library. The suite enables users to seamlessly search and discover articles to accelerate their comprehension of complex technical papers.

The system surfaces deep insights, replacing the typical keyword queries with natural, conversational research workflows.

As AI tools become more common in conducting research, IEEE collaborated to build the suite around a simple principle: Answers should be trustworthy, not just fast, says W. Clem Karl, vice president, IEEE Publication Services and Products.

“AI can be a highly effective and beneficial tool that can help researchers accelerate discovery, enhance decision-making, and surface new connections,” Karl says. “However, many AI engines present a great risk of hallucinating answers or introducing bias into otherwise credible research. With this in mind, IEEE has taken a responsible approach in our AI strategy by developing concrete safeguards to ensure our solution is rigorously grounded in scientific evidence that users can trust.

“As stewards of the scholarly record, we held the new AI engine to the same standards as the peer-reviewed research we publish: A researcher shouldn’t have to trust an answer; they should be able to verify the work behind it.”

The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite was developed in close collaboration with global scientific and library communities.

The development process began with research into user needs and the challenges associated with existing AI research assistants. More than 3,000 testers—including engineers, scientists, and library information professionals—provided feedback to refine the AI engine and support research workflows.

To mitigate the risk of AI hallucinations, the search-retrieval process is limited to querying the millions of IEEE peer-reviewed full-text documents, alongside an expertly curated dataset of STEM metadata. If the AI tool is unable to find relevant scientific content within the defined dataset, it is designed to inform the user rather than generate fabricated answers.

“IEEE is committed to providing the technical community with a highly precise and reliable research experience,” says Steven Heffner, IEEE’s chief publication officer and managing director of IEEE Publications. “The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite offers something unique in that it is the only AI research assistant that leverages both the full-text and metadata of IEEE’s peer-reviewed content, rather than abstracts alone.

“The difference is significant: Our internal testing showed a threefold increase in result quality and accuracy across every key metric. These results underscore how critical full-text grounding is for technical research.”

For more information about features and coverage, or to request a demo for your organization, visit the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite website.

Claire Olini is the senior manager for IEEE Corporate and Strategic Product Launch and Engagement.

Michael Spada is director of IEEE Product Launch and Engagement Strategy.

#3296. Nintendo's Black Friday Deals Are Actually Pretty Good

Black Friday is nearly upon us. From now through Cyber Monday, retailers and companies alike are offering deals and discounts on their wares. While I always keep an eye out for Nintendo deals offered by stores like Amazon and Best Buy, it seems the company is offering its own discounts this year—and, surprisingly, they're actually pretty solid.

On Thursday, Nintendo announced its Black Friday discounts. We've already seen Switch 2 sales ahead of the Black Friday season, but now, Nintendo has confirmed an official discount for the console. Starting Nov. 22 through Dec. 5, you can pick up Nintendo's Switch 2 Mario Kart bundle for $499.99, down $50 from $549.99. That includes the console, a download of Mario Kart World, and a 90-day Nintendo Switch Online Individual Membership.

If you already have a Switch 2 console and/or Mario Kart World, you're not left out of the Black Friday deals here. From Nov. 22 through Nov. 29, Nintendo is also running discounts on several high-profile Switch and Switch 2 games. During this promotion, each of the following is $39.99:

Super Mario Galaxy + Super Mario Galaxy 2

Nintendo rarely offers official discounts on some of its biggest titles, especially in this current era. Games like Donkey Kong Bananza retail for upwards of $69.99, so you're saving as much as $30 on these games during this week-long promotion. In addition, Nintendo announced a sale on its digital store that runs from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2, though it didn't say which titles would be on sale. Just keep an eye on all these dates: The Switch 2 console promotion runs longer than the physical and digital games discounts, while the digital sale runs longer than the physical sale.

Nintendo says that these discounts will be available "at select retailers," as well as its brick-and-mortar locations in New York and San Francisco. You can also buy the Switch 2 bundle through Nintendo's website.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Use price tracking tools to determine if the deals you're keeping tabs on are actually a deal. If you feel like that's too much work, we already do that for you, so follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products makes you focus and make smarter decisions.

#3295. watchOS 27.3: Three new features coming soon to Apple Watch

watchOS 27.3 will launch to all users next month and introduce these three new Apple Watch features.

Siri AI keeps getting new features and also expanding to more languages. And in watchOS 27.3, the assistant will improve in both categories.

watchOS 27.3 upgrades Siri AI with new app actions across built-in apps like Calendar, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, and Weather. With these capabilities, Siri on your wrist can do more than ever.

There are also four new Siri AI languages supported in watchOS 27.3: Chinese (traditional), Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

For the latest Apple Watch models, watchOS 27.3 adds a new Audio Intelligence feature called Live Rewind. Per Apple’s website:

Live Rewind recalls what was just said in the last 15 seconds by showing a text snippet on your Apple Watch when you double-press the Digital Crown, so you can catch something you missed or are less familiar with. You can ask Siri about the content of the snippet or simply save it to the Siri app.

I’m curious to see how useful this proves in everyday life. When Apple demoed the feature in September, it showed Live Rewind being used at a restaurant when an Apple Watch user missed part of the server’s menu explanation. Asking the server to repeat what they said seems like an easier solution, but perhaps there are other occasions Live Rewind will come in handy.

It won’t be for everyone, but I’ve been testing watchOS 27.3’s new Siri Recap feature and really love it.

Siri Recap only works on Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and it’s off by default. But if you have one of those models and enable the feature, Siri can create automatic logs of what’s happening in your day-to-day life.

Most of the time, you won’t need to reference any of the recaps and they’ll be automatically deleted after a week. But based on my experience with the feature, Siri Recap definitely comes in handy at times when trying to remember key details from conversations.

Which of watchOS 27.3’s new features are you most interested in? Let us know in the comments.

#3294. Nvidia CEO is out, but how will it impact you? Live analysis on AI bubble, chip production and AMD after Jensen Huang resignation

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has just resigned, but you already knew that. What you may not know is how removing the AI kingmaker will impact you?

The consensus seems to be unanimous amongst the many experts we've talked to: things will stay the same in the short term for consumers, but the long-term is going to look very different.

Could a more financially-minded Interim CEO take the choice to pivot harder to data centers? What happens to the AI bubble now the de facto leader at the top has gone after admitting to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, and then being caught in another?

While there's a salacious story here that's fit for a Netflix drama, I'm more focused on that. Let's find out together live. But first, some context.

In 2025, US intelligence officials briefed Donald Trump regarding Jensen Huang’s close relationship with Alice Huang (no relation). Huang is an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company. US officials began watching her under the suspicion she’s smuggling Nvidia’s AI chips into China.

Spring 2026: A memo drafted by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio circulates among top policymakers in the Trump administration — explicitly stating that the Megaspeed executive is a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security.

In May 2026, despite these concerns being circulated regarding Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese asset, he was invited to join Trump’s official delegation during a diplomatic trip to China.

At September’s White House State Dinner, Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, attended the dinner hosted by Trump for Chinese President Xi Jinping. The Huangs are seated at the top table alongside Trump, Xi and then-Apple CEO Tim Cook.

In October, the intelligence became public. The New York Times published a report detailing the 2025 intelligence briefings, putting these initial allegations into the public sphere.

November 2026, a second extramarital affair came to light following another New York Times article claiming Huang engaged in a relationship with Nvidia employee Kimberly Powell. Following a discussion with the board, Jensen Huang resigned as CEO.

Nvidia's board has 11 members, including Huang, that are meeting today to consider whether to dismiss Jensen from his position following an internal investigation launched on November 8.

The ten other board members are independent and have the power to fire the CEO on the grounds of breaking the company's ethical standards. We are expecting a result to be announced later today on the verdict they've reached — even if that verdict is a further delay.

Quite possibly. According to an exclusive report from the Wall Street Journal, Nvidia's board "is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang" and that it would leave "one of the world’s most valuable companies in need of a new leader."

However, there's no immediate successor who could replace the leather jacket-wearing CEO who has become the face of the current AI arms race.

Dan Ives, a tech analyst at Wedbush Securities described Huang as the "central nervous system" of the U.S. technology ecosystem. Ives went as far as calling him "irreplaceable" and warned that losing him would disrupt not just Nvidia, but the broader tech ecosystem. According to Ives, should Huang leave Nvidia, his immediate exit could trigger a 25%–30% stock drop.

This saga hit critical mass when The New York Times published a report detailing a long timeline of Huang’s alleged affair with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.

Following this report, Jensen admitted to an affair in an internal email to his staff, and while he didn’t outright admit it was with Alice Huang, the fact he spent part of his statement talking about “national security concerns,” and that he’s “proud and grateful to be an American,” seems to connect the dots.

I owe my family and all of you an apology.

I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.

Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.

To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.

To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.

Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.

Nvidia operates a famously flat structure with Jensen Huang actively involved in the company's routine operations. That said, one analyst told me his departure today is unlikely to torpedo the company's current AI focus.

"A prolonged leadership crisis could also disrupt product development or investment, but I think Jensen Huang's departure is unlikely to have any immediate effect on the price or availability of Nvidia products," said Louise Wooldridge, Senior Research Manager, Games, Ampere Analysis.

"There is also the possibility that, if Nvidia's competitive position is weakened by Huang leaving, other chipmakers (like AMD) could gain an advantage, and this stronger competition could improve the landscape for consumers.

"Overall, though, I think the commercial incentives pushing Nvidia towards AI will remain, regardless of the leadership situation, and so it is more likely that little will change in the long run."

Jensen Huang has announced his resignation as Nvidia's CEO.

Nvidia has confirmed that, following Huang's departure, Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer will step into the role of Interim Chief Executive Officer.

"Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named," Nvidia said.

"The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates."

In a press release announcing Huang's departure, Colette Kress, Interim CEO and CFO of Nvidia said: "I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years.”

“We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.”

The press release ended by saying the Nvidia Board and the company "thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry."

The market isn't going to officially open until 9:30 am, but Nvidia shares have already fallen 10% in U.S. premarket trading after Huang's exit was announced.

Nvidia is one of the "Magnificent Seven" tech stocks, along with the likes of Apple, Amazon and Alphabet, that collectively make up over 30% of the S&P 500. A lot of standard 401(k) plans are heavily weighted in index funds that are tied to the performance of these companies. So today's news could have a knock-on effect for a lot of people.

So, who is the new Interim CEO of Nvidia? Colette Kress joined the company in September 2013 and is the executive vice president and chief financial officer. She has previously served nearly 25 years in a range of finance roles at major technology companies, including 13 years at Microsoft.

“Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” said Harvey Jones, the newly-appointed chair of the Nvidia Board of Directors.

“She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing Nvidia’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.”

As U.S. markets open for the day, Nvidia's stock price is jumping up and down. I saw it open at 13% down before recovering somewhat to 8% down at the time of this writing but it's set to be a turbulent day for Wall Street.

Nvidia is the lynchpin of the current AI boom and demand for its chips has seen the company become one of the most valuable companies in the world. Today's news isn't going to change that but with investor confidence in AI expenditure starting to waver, we could see some long-term fallout further down the line.

"In the near-term, I think Nvidia will continue to perform as usual. The fundamentals won't change for CY 2027 and potentially CY 2028. A lot of these deals and supply chain are already locked up, Ryuta Makino, software and semiconductor analyst at Gabelli Funds, told Tom's Guide.

"The longer-term, post Feynman is where I would watch for. So 2029 and 2030 are years that may be impacted more broadly. There is potential that this will lower AI infrastructure spend in the long-term given that Nvidia will likely lose market share.

"This can also mean that lower efficiency gains on these servers equals lower AI efficiency and therefore the entire ecosystem will be worse overall. I am still assessing the impact but there will definitely be a ripple."

While this is going on, we're keeping an eye on Nvidia's stock price as the market absorbs the news. Opening at 13% down — wiping more than half a trillion dollars off the company's market value — it now appears to be sitting at 6% down.

Nvidia is set to report its latest financial results next Tuesday.

There's some stinging reaction to Jensen Huang's departure now coming through.

Writing on Substack, scientist Gary Marcus, stated bluntly: “He had to go. He enabled and even lobbied for Chinese AI, subverted US policy, and carelessly left himself vulnerable to both blackmail and espionage.”

"He also left Nvidia open to endless litigation and investigation, which is perhaps part of why they encouraged him to go, despite his enormous talents."

Nvidia's new Interim CEO, Colette Kress, has just sent an internal memo to the company, as reported by Reuters:

I believe deeply in this company and in its future. More than anything, I believe in each of you, in our customers and partners and in the vital role we play every day in the global economy. The Board, Estaff (Executive Staff) and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication. Thank you. This company has achieved so much because of the work that all of you bring to it every single day. You are our greatest strength. You will hear more from leadership in the coming days about our future together, and we will host a company meeting on November 18 at 9am PT. We play a vital role in building the technology that is powering the AI revolution, and we have important work ahead of us. So let’s move forward together, with the same determination and commitment that have always defined this company.

In that transition announcement, it was also noted that Harvey Jones, an Nvidia board member since 1993, has been appointed as the first chair of the company's board of directors.

I am writing to share an important update. Jensen has resigned as CEO and Board Member, and the Board has asked our Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress to serve as interim CEO while it conducts a search for a permanent successor looking at both internal and external candidates. I will serve as the first-ever Chair of the Board.

As CFO for over 13 years, Colette has been a key architect of NVIDIA’s growth and capital strategy. She possesses a deep understanding of this business and the markets in which we operate. The Board has full confidence in Colette to deliver on our commitments to shareholders, customers, partners, and to each of you.

Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. We pioneered accelerated computing, defined the modern GPU, and built the platform that powered artificial intelligence.

The Board takes seriously our duty as stewards of this great company.

The strength of this company resides in our employees, leadership team, technical strength and partner ecosystem. I am confident that under Colette’s leadership, with the full support of the Board, we will continue to grow our business, and lead the industry forward. Thank you for your focus, your professionalism, and your commitment to NVIDIA.

So now we know the news — the world knows the news and the memes have been splendid. But the question on everyone's lips is a simple one: what happens now?

The AI bubble was starting to show cracks. Does this pop it? That's what we're going to analyze and see what happens.

Because you've got an equal amount of people saying "it's over," as saying "this won't change anything."

Kieren Jessop, Principal Analyst in Omidia's PC team has told Tom's Guide that "nothing will change for consumers next month," but warns that "I'd be more cautious about the next two to three years."

"Consumer is now a small share of Nvidia’s revenue, but strategically it’s the on-ramp: PC users and gamers are how a generation of developers got onto the platform.

Local AI inference on PCs is a growing workload, led by businesses that want sensitive data kept in-house, more predictable costs than per-use cloud pricing and lower latency, with consumers likely to follow later."

In Jessop's own words, Huang "treated that link as strategic," while an interim CEO from finance may be more "likely to focus on data center customers," which would mean "fewer new consumer initiatives."

"The exposed areas are the follow-through: Nvidia’s first Windows-on-Arm PC chip only reached laptops last month and still has software compatibility work outstanding, and the next GeForce generation has reportedly slipped to 2028.

Founders have come back before, Steve Jobs being the obvious example, Altman the more recent example, but whether Huang does is unknowable at this stage. Either way, the risk isn’t that Nvidia products get worse; it’s that fewer ambitious ones get launched while the question is open."

...yea I'm just as confused as you are. President Trump has just posted on Truth Social about who he thinks should be CEO of Nvidia next.

We've got a reaction from Avi Greengart, expert consumer technology analyst over at Techsponential!

"In the near term, nothing changes for consumers because Nvidia’s GPU allocation is largely set — and data centers are still the priority, not gaming and client computing," Greengart commented.

"The bigger issue for consumers is the rise in cost of memory and storage due to the AI build out, and Nvidia doesn’t play a direct role there at all. But Nvidia really did run entirely through Jensen, so a change the top absolutely can affect the company’s strategy in the mid and long-term."

It's easy to talk so casually about stock prices in the percentage terms. Like "oh no, shares went down 10%," but what does that actually mean.

Since the news of the first affair, Nvidia has lost $888 billion in market value so far.

That would be the equivalent of the following companies all going to zero overnight:

Is that all? No! Because it's way more than that. Nvidia lost double that amount over the past few days. So take the remaining $451 billion (roughly) and set it on fire, then you'll get what Team Green sank by.

I can only imagine it's been a four-day party for the company board and investors. They're up 5.7% today alone amidst Jensen's exit.

@WSJ Yiu can't do this to me. I build this company brick by brick. https://t.co/aDsipLBxEnNovember 12, 2026

There's been many AI-generated memes, but as a Spider-Man fan, this has to be my favorite!

We have more analysis — this time from eMarketer senior analyst, Asa Hiken:

“Jensen Huang’s resignation is a watershed moment for Nvidia, which now has to prove it can maintain its AI dominance without the leader largely responsible for building it. And given the broader AI industry’s heavy dependence on Nvidia’s chips, Huang’s departure introduces uncertainty well beyond the company itself.”

“While Huang’s personal decisions are scandalous, his particular affair with an alleged Chinese spy raises much bigger questions about the security risks facing companies at the center of the AI race. AI technology has become critical to US national security, making even the personal relationships of industry leaders a potential vulnerability.”

"Jensen was also AI’s chief cheerleader with global politicians; without him we’ll see how Nvidia manages Trump’s last two years in office and increasing tensions with China and Taiwan.

Nvidia under Jensen was also a key funder for the circular ecosystem of AI foundation model makers, hardware and networking gear, and deployment partners that supercharged datacenter growth.

The interim CEO was the CFO for these deals, but Jensen signed them, and a new CEO may take a less aggressive approach, especially with pressure against data centers becoming a major political issue and investors worrying about a bubble."

As we're hearing from experts, nothing will change in the short-term. But panic is setting in among PC builders on socials that Nvidia might take this leadership vacuum as an excuse to abandon GeForce entirely.

Because the numbers unfortunately back-up a pivot if someone financially-minded was to take a look. Gaming makes up 7.4% of Nvidia's total revenue.

Once they became the picks and shovels company for the AI gold rush, it was no longer a gaming company; it became a data center company.

And as PC Gamer points out, "Nvidia would be foolish to put more focus on gaming hardware while the AI cash cow continues to provide."

While he became the AI kingmaker, Jensen Huang was also integral to the growth of PC gaming — no matter how you swing it. Now he's out, and with an Interim CEO in town, this could change.

We're starting to see reactions from Washington, and they all seem to be unanimous: strong chip export controls are needed — not just on the physical chips but on access to remote cloud compute.

And if that happens, the global total addressable market (TAM) of the silicon providers gets locked down, and the sudden drop would impact the big three memory makers (SK Hynix, Micron, Samsung).

My prediction if this happens: Wafer capacity is rebalanced in the face of this reduced capacity, and the valuation of AI changes significantly. That doesn't mean immediately lower prices on consumer PC hardware, as a lot of these costs are locked in. But the money has to come from somewhere.

#3293. Google Gemini for CarPlay now available

Google’s Gemini AI chatbot app for Apple CarPlay is now available. The company confirmed that it is bringing the full Gemini Live conversation experience to CarPlay on Wednesday, and the app update arrived on Thursday.

Google bringing Gemini to CarPlay is especially notable for one reason. Gemini was the last major AI chatbot holdout.

CarPlay has supported AI chatbot apps and other conversational apps for a while now.

iPhone apps including ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, Copilot, Meta AI, and Grok all shipped CarPlay support already. Siri includes a standalone app in iOS 27, which also supports CarPlay.

Google has previously supported Gemini features through Google Maps on CarPlay, but not the Gemini Live experience through the dedicated chatbot app.

“Gemini on Apple CarPlay is rolling out globally starting today to all Gemini users on iOS across every supported Gemini Live language,” Google says.

“To get started, make sure you’ve updated to the latest version of the Gemini app on your iPhone, enabled microphone permissions, and used Gemini Live on your phone at least once. The next time you connect your phone to your car, tap the Gemini icon on your CarPlay display, then start a new conversation or pick up a recent one.”

Google Gemini for CarPlay is now available through the iPhone App Store.
