As Yellowjackets fans brace for the beginning of the end, the cast came together to celebrate and mourn the series at the final season premiere.

On Sunday, the stars of the supernatural survival thriller shared with Deadline that it’s been “quite heartbreaking” and “bittersweet” concluding the show with Season 4, which premieres Nov. 20 on Paramount+ with Premium Plan. Watch the trailer below.

“It’s been wonderful. I mean, I was not ready for it to end,” said Melanie Lynskey, who stars as Shauna Shipman. “I didn’t want it to end, but here we are. So, I was grateful when we were going through it that we knew it was the ending, that it wasn’t just, we were filming and thinking we were all gonna reunite in another year. I was grateful that we knew.”

Sophie Nélisse, who plays her teen counterpart, agree that the final season has been “bittersweet,” adding, “I think we were all looking forward to seeing what this show will bring us in our future careers, and everyone finding their niche and finding what speaks to them after this. But also, just really weird. I feel like I grew up with all of these coworkers.” Watch on Deadline

RELATED: 2026 TV Cancellations Photo Gallery: Series Ending This Year & Beyond

“And so it feels like we’ve all evolved so much, both as actors and as humans,” she added. “So, it felt weird because I think every time we wrapped a season, there was this reassurance that would see each other again. We’re like, ‘It’s a goodbye, but not really.’ And this feels very final and decisive, and that’s quite heartbreaking.”

Jasmin Savoy Brown on cherishing every moment of the final season of #Yellowjackets and Tai’s arc in Season 4: “I think I got one of the best storylines this season” pic.twitter.com/fIDuk9kyuw

Sophie Thatcher, who is back as teen Natalie Scatorccio, found the experience “really surreal, but it was nice that we knew going in. We could kind of process things as they were happening. I felt like I wasn’t ready to let go of Natalie, and I waited to read the last episodes, because I didn’t want it to be real.”

Jasmin Savoy Brown, the actress who plays teen Taissa Turner, noted that the foresight of the final season “made every moment extra heightened. It’s seven years of our lives. Some of these girls are the age now that I was when we shot the pilot. They were literally 17, and now they’re 25, 26. They came of age… it’s crazy.”

Liv Hewson, who plays Van Palmer, explained that she “really wanted to be as present as possible, and I wanted to make the most of it. This show is so unique and this opportunity is so rare, and I just wanted to make the most of this opportunity, make the most of the time we had together, and make the most of getting to live in this world with these characters. I wanted to do as much as possible. And I think I did everything I could have done, and I’m proud of that.”

Sophie Thatcher shares how she waited to read the final #Yellowjackets scripts for Season 4: “I wasn’t ready to let go of Natalie” pic.twitter.com/0FFeTyqC7F

Samantha Hanratty, who stars a Misty Quigley agreed with her co-stars that it was “a huge gift to know that we were gonna have an ending.”

“I feel like so many shows nowadays never get answers, and unfortunately they don’t get to finish. Well, we got to have our start, our middle, our end, and I’m really excited for everybody to see,” she continued. “I’m just proud, honestly. I’m so sad to say goodbye to these characters. I’m not ready, I don’t think I’m there yet, and that’s OK. Maybe when the finale comes out, I’ll be a little bit better to say goodbye. But it was a very tearjerking ending for all of us.

Nia Sondaya, who plays Akilah, said she “was really able to make the most of every moment this season, and I really got to savor spending time with all my castmates and just really enjoying this season. So honestly, it was bittersweet but overall a great experience for me going in and getting to do this.”

Jenna Burgess, who plays Melissa, is still adjusting to the end, “I mean, it hasn’t even hit me that we’re not doing this again—oh my god, maybe it just hit me right now. But this show will always challenge you as a person and as an actor, because we’re telling the story of real people and humans and just trauma, lots of trauma. So just taking care of yourself, knowing that it’s going to be wild.”

Jenna Burgess on the “bittersweet” experience of wrapping on #Yellowjackets pic.twitter.com/GpDrauGR9c

Elijah Wood, who reprises his role as Walter Tattersall, felt “so privileged” to join the show in Season 2. “I really genuinely am a fan of the show, I loved that first season. It was a treat to be asked to come and join and play in that sandbox with this extraordinary cast, to work with Christina [Ricci] again,” he said. “So, going back with a real satisfying way to say goodbye to the character was just a joy, a real joy. And again, it’s bittersweet. I think for everybody involved, it’s been a real fun ride, and I don’t think anybody wanted to see it go. But all great things must come to an end, you know?”

Following last year’s news that the show’s fourth season would be its final season, co-creator Bart Nickerson explained that he and Ashley Lyle “had always given the caveat that we felt like the show would tell us when it wanted to end.”

“And just in the breaking of this story, it started to feel like we were sort of moving toward the end more rapidly,” added Nickerson earlier this week. “So then, the decision became, ‘OK, do we try to squeeze a lot into Season 4 or run the risk of overstaying our welcome with a fifth season?’ We chose to try to squeeze it in.”

In Yellowjackets, a 1996 New Jersey soccer team’s plane crashes in the Canadian wilderness, where they struggle to survive while they’re stranded for 19 months as a dark supernatural force seemingly lurks in the woods. Meanwhile, their adult counterparts cope with the memories of what went down in the wilderness.

Premiering Nov. 20, the fourth and final season sees the Yellowjackets rescued and returned home, where they must adjust to civilization and take their secret to the grave.

#3267. ‘Today’ Co-Host Savannah Guthrie Extends NBC News Contract

Savannah Guthrie has extended her contract at NBC News to remain as Today co-host, a source familiar with the matter confirmed on Thursday.

The morning show, approaching its 75th anniversary in January, beat ABC’s Good Morning America and CBS Mornings in total viewers and the 25-54 demo last season, taking the top spot in both categories for the first time in 14 years.

Guthrie has been co-host of Today since 2012, and currently is joined by Craig Melvin.

Her re-signing at the network comes amid the personal and harrowing ordeal of the disappearance of her mother, Nancy, from her Tucson home in February. Authorities later released security camera video of a masked person at Nancy Guthrie‘s front door, but they have not identified any suspects in her abduction. Savannah Guthrie has continued to call for any information on what happened.

Guthrie also has been an anchor during NBC’s Olympics coverage, including of opening ceremonies, and moderated a town hall with Donald Trump just weeks before the 2020 presidential election. Watch on Deadline

Breaker first reported on Guthrie’s contract extension.

#3265. Gentler Streak 6.0 adds a new wellbeing timeline and customizable dashboard

In an update rolling out today, Gentler Streak is introducing new ways for users to track their wellbeing and personalize the app’s guidance based on how they feel. Here are the details.

One of my favorite exercise-tracking apps got even better today with an update that expands its functionality beyond workouts and fitness metrics to better reflect how users actually feel.

Starting today, Gentler Streak will let users log how they feel each day, including their mood, symptoms, and other factors that may not be reflected in their health and fitness data.

Some days, the way we feel isn’t reflected in what the data says, no matter the data quality. “How I Feel” captures the part that devices can’t grasp: personal context. And how you feel is not only a mood: it is also a sore throat, heavy legs or a poor night’s sleep. The feature was inspired by the Gentler Streak community, including people living with chronic fatigue, fibromyalgia, ADHD, and those not wearing their Apple Watch at night. Without overnight signals, their guidance has less to work with.

According to the team behind Gentler Streak, these new features are aimed at users whose health and fitness data may not accurately reflect how they feel, including those dealing with chronic conditions, menopause, stress, or poor sleep.

In practice, the app will now feature four tabs: Today, Health, Workouts, and Insights. In the Today and Health tabs, a new “Anything to add?” field will let users rate how they feel, from Great to Off, and add context about what might be affecting their well-being, including fatigue, feeling calm, or custom tags.

You decide when the prompt appears. Go to Profile > Settings > Self-Evaluation Prompt and choose one of three options: only when your vitals or sleep are off, always on, or never.

Gentler Stories notes that the self-assessments will override the app’s wellbeing estimates for that day, with its daily guidance adjusting accordingly.

The Today tab will also feature an expanded 10- or 30-day timeline showing logged workouts, wellbeing estimates, potential symptoms, poor sleep or vitals, and the first day of a menstrual period, while Health will introduce an interactive chart showing users how their wellbeing changes over time, with the ability to filter by symptoms.

Users can now also customize which information appears on their Today screen, including vitals, sleep, steps, menstrual cycle, VO₂ max, and workouts, which is a nice touch.

For users who are sick, injured, or taking a break from exercise, the app’s hallmark Activity Path will make way for a new Wellbeing Path, which lets them track their wellbeing on a daily basis.

For users with Active status, a new colorful wellbeing line will appear beneath the Activity Path, reflecting how they feel each day. This information is logged automatically for those who wear their Apple Watch overnight, or based on self-assessments for those who don’t.

Importantly, Gentler Stories notes that all information entered through the new feature remains on the user’s device, with no accounts or company-operated servers involved.

Gentler Streak is available for free on the App Store, with in-app purchases for monthly, yearly, family, and lifetime subscriptions.

#3264. Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream

Nearly 70 percent of respondents say they want an AI assistant in their next device, according to a new report

Qualcomm builds intelligent, connected, computing and AI solutions that transform industries and advance human progress.

A recent report by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide, shows that around 70 percent of respondents express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.

This article is brought to you by Qualcomm Technologies.

For many consumers, much of the promise and appeal of AI is personal. Consumers are looking past generic tools and want to know how these technologies will help them in their daily lives. These trends coincide with the advent of new classes of wearable devices that, in addition to being able to leverage powerful frontier models, feature built-in intelligence that understand the context of a user. Where are they? What are they seeing and hearing? What are their habits, their preferences, their schedules?

It’s an astonishing pivot, from passive accessories that served mostly to send users smartphone notifications to proactive, intelligent companions. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. And it shifts the focus toward you, the user.

These new technologies are exciting. But what do consumers really want?

A Personal AI report, commissioned by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide (the U.S., U.K., Germany, India, Brazil, and China) focused on the rise of personal AI in intelligent wearables looks deeply at these developments.

The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI.

Survey respondents are less interested in single devices and are responding more to the idea of connected ecosystems. As people expand their roster of devices, it only makes sense. Instead of relying entirely on a smartphone and a laptop, respondents also have connected technology in their cars, as well as intelligent wearables like smartwatches, smart glasses, hearables, and other wearables like rings, pins, and pendants. They want those devices to work in concert, and the way to do that is to decentralize any single one of them. Instead, the AI agent that knows the user and works across all of those devices becomes the unifying factor.

Consider a typical workday: A user’s watch detects it is time to leave for a meeting and, with permission, their AI agent factors in calendar details, real-time traffic and battery status across their devices. In the car, it suggests the best route and briefs them on their meeting agenda. As they arrive, smart glasses surface a discreet reminder, such as the meeting location or the name of a new contact, while the phone stays in their pocket. No one device has to do everything; each plays the role it is best suited for, coordinated by a personal AI agent that understands the user’s context and acts only at the user’s direction.

With this in mind, simply adding more hardware to the mix isn’t sufficient. Even though respondents will be open to new form factors, they’ll demand more from their ecosystem of devices. They’ll be sensitive to points of friction and needless complexity, and they’ll require each new device to bring something new to the table — “incremental intelligence, convenience, or contextual awareness that their existing devices cannot deliver on their own what the report,” reads the report.

The usage trends are up. The report found that those who own wearables are already using AI frequently (60 percent use it at least weekly), which indicates that it’s becoming less of a fun experiment for early adopters and more of a critical mass habit.

The “always-on” nature of intelligent wearables appears to be winning respondents, too. The report found the following statistics on average continuous wear among users:

But for all the excitement and engagement around intelligent wearables, there’s a gating factor: trust. As use cases for intelligent wearables expands to more personal and persistent experiences, trust is a necessity for Personal AI.

Notably, the report found that respondents expressed more interest in adopting intelligent wearables when Snapdragon was introduced as the enabling platform. This reinforces the value of having an established, trusted technology foundation in the mix.

The report shows that consumer appetite for AI is high, with 60-70 percent of those surveyed expressing interest in advanced AI as they consider a new device. That’s a constant. But remaining purchase drivers differed between device categories.

Audio playback quality is the most influential purchase driver for true wireless earbuds and headphones. For smartwatches, it’s display quality and responsiveness. Respondents are less concerned about technical specifications than aesthetics like materials and finish when it comes to devices like smart rings and pendants. And for smart glasses, it’s all about the type of control, whether it’s voice, gesture, or touch.

Artificial intelligence is entering a new phase, one that is deeply personal, continuously present, and seamlessly embedded into the devices we wear every day. This evolution, which we define as “Personal AI”, represents a shift away from generic, cloud-only intelligence toward AI that understands individuals in context: their habits, preferences, environments, and intent, in real time.

Alongside these purchase drivers is another key finding: Consumer appetite for Personal AI agents has gone mainstream. The report says that 70 percent of respondents “express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.” With each individual as the center of their own ecosystem, voice becomes the most critical, natural method for interacting with agents.

Intelligent wearables comprise much of the hardware of this “ecosystem of you.” Consumers are interested in ecosystems instead of single devices, and they’re looking for agentic AI capabilities that understand and act on their behalf.

Yet so much of the industry remains undefined. OEMs and technology makers have an enormous opportunity right now to innovate and iterate on the strong technological foundations that platform makers are building. And the roadmap for what consumers want is clear.

All percentages, consumer behaviors, and attitudes stated in this report are based only on the responses of the individuals who participated in our survey.

Qualcomm Technologies is a global leader in communications and computing technologies, including leading-edge AI, high-performance, low-power computing, and connectivity solutions. Headquartered in San Diego, Calif., the company develops technologies for next-generation mobile networks and smart devices, and designs semiconductors such as mobile processors and AI chips.

Between the sleek frames and seamless Mandarin translation, Google made tech on my face feel surprisingly invisible

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The moment Google’s new smart glasses started to make sense to me, I was talking to a woman I’ve never met before about what she likes to eat in Shenzhen.

She was speaking Mandarin, and I was speaking English. We were having the kind of conversation I’d want to have with someone I’m getting to know: What’s your hometown like? What traditional food should I try? And where in New York might I be able to get a taste of it?

I’ve used live translation on smart glasses (and phones, and earbuds in the past.) But this conversation, part of a demonstration of Google’s new collection of Intelligent Eyewear, felt the most inherently natural. After just a handful of exchanges, both the language barrier and the hardware helping me cross it felt nearly invisible.

That’s a promising start for a product that needs to work hard to give people a compelling reason to wear a camera and AI assistant on their face. Google’s bet combines Gemini’s ability to understand what you’re looking at, connections to the apps you already use and, through Gentle Monster’s and Warby Parker’s fashion footprints, glasses you might actually want to wear.

To that last point, looking good certainly helps. But at a time when people are understandably anxious about how camera glasses could be misused, making them look more ordinary also raises questions about how easily everyone else can recognize them.

After trying Google’s smart glasses (not to be confused with Google Glass) for a few hours, here’s what impressed me, and where I still have questions.

The collections were developed with Samsung, with Warby Parker’s frames starting at $395 and Gentle Monster’s at $449. Preorders open November 12, with in-store and online availability beginning December 10. The glasses work with supported Pixel, Samsung Galaxy and iPhone models, although some features are Android-only at launch.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

I care about the effectiveness of technology. But I also care very much about how something looks on my face.

With Gentle Monster and Warby Parker involved, Google has a wide selection of frames, colors and lenses that made me feel more like I was choosing eyewear than choosing a gadget and accepting whatever style comes with it.

Some of the frames I tried looked even less obviously like smart glasses than Meta’s. From a style perspective, I appreciate that

Gentle Monster’s collection includes six designs, with colors including dark red, pink, gray and yellow, plus prescription options for most frames. Warby Parker offers three styles — Alden, Reid and Wren — with different widths, prescription options and optical or sun lenses. Google puts all of the frames’ weight at around 41 grams.

I’m already a self-proclaimed Gentle Monster stan, so I was particularly interested in how its distinctive design personality would translate to smart glasses. I found more than a few I could see myself wearing every day.

Some of the frames I tried looked even less obviously like smart glasses than Meta’s. From a style perspective, I appreciate that. From the perspective of someone standing in front of the camera, it’s more complicated. The same design that makes a wearer feel comfortable could make it harder for someone else to recognize that recording is possible. I think both things can be true.

Google discussed a number of safeguards during my briefing, including restrictions intended to prevent camera use when the recording indicator is covered.

The outward-facing LED lights up when you capture a photo or video for your gallery. Sensors are designed to detect if that indicator is covered or tampered with and prevent capture.

The glasses are also designed to redact bystanders’ faces before sending images to Gemini, and Google says the camera visuals used for those AI interactions aren’t saved in Gemini History or used for AI training or ad targeting.

Unlike Meta, Google’s sphere of influence includes the places people shop for accessories, the ads promoting them and the apps that can access the camera. Its stated protections include banning accessories designed to conceal recording lights from Shopping and Ads, and prohibiting apps that enable real-time facial identification through Google Play. It can also monitor YouTube for any “educational” tampering content.

I wouldn’t say this automatically makes Google more trustworthy in this budding wearable face-off against Meta. But it gives the company more places to intervene and more responsibility to follow through.

Google’s other advantage over Meta is the quality of its AI assistant. In my demo, I experienced ways to connect what Gemini sees via the camera with information and actions. For example, interpreting a bulletin and helping add an event to a calendar, or translating a cookbook and answering follow-up questions about it.

I could keep a conversation going without repeating a wake word for every question. Furthermore, during instructional interactions such as learning how to throw a football with proper spiral or giving myself a quick tarot reading, Gemini stayed on standby waiting for me to proceed step-by-step.

The connections to Google’s apps could give that convenience more substance. Calendar entries, Gmail and Google Photos are already parts of my day. How reliably the glasses can work across those services is something I’ll need more time to test, including which features depend on your phone and setup.

Of all the Google intelligent eyewear experiences I tried, Live Translation made the strongest impression.

The translated audio had a female-sounding voice and seemed to follow the speaker’s pace and rhythm. It felt more connected to the person standing in front of me than a generic voice reading back a sentence.

Google Translate supports real-time speech translation across more than 70 languages on the glasses. My English-to-Mandarin conversation offered a small but compelling glimpse of what that could mean in practice.

The translated audio had a female-sounding voice and seemed to follow the speaker’s pace and rhythm. It felt more connected to the person standing in front of me than a generic voice reading back a sentence.

Sure, there was still a bit of a delay. At first, we needed a little time to work out when to speak and when to listen. But after a couple of exchanges, that friction became less distracting.

The conversation itself also mattered. This was a demo, and the person helping me was clearly familiar with the experience. But I was able to steer it toward the questions I wanted to ask, including my favorite subject of food.

Overall, the exchange felt responsive and engaging from my side, and I wanted to keep talking. That’s a more meaningful and authentic first impression than successfully translating one rehearsed sentence.

For all the attention on AI features and live translation and cameras, in practice, I mostly use smart glasses as headphones.

In my demo listening to music, vocals sounded clear and I liked how the audio was positioned around my ears. I also tried the swipe-and tap-based music controls located on the right side of the frame, which are part of the less flashy experience I’d expect to use constantly.

Google lists support for YouTube Music, Spotify and Apple Music, along with Audible on Android at launch. You can also take calls and respond to messages hands-free.

That said, I noticed quite a bit of sound leakage at higher volumes, being a demo space with other people testing out the glasses. I don’t yet know whether the amount varies by frame style or fit, but it was noticeable enough during the demonstration to be worth flagging.

The camera is familiar territory if you’ve used Meta’s glasses. It’s a 12MP ultrawide camera, and you can ask the assistant to take a photo or use the physical capture button.

I tried taking pictures outside around Little Island, and they came out… okay. For my standards, I wouldn’t expect glasses to ever replace a flagship phone camera. But there is attraction to having a hands-free way to capture your perspective without stopping to hold up a phone.

As is the case with Meta glasses, I’d imagine the rated 9 hours of battery life will be cut back by frequent camera usage. There is an included charging case that provides up to seven recharges.

Google’s intelligent eyewear has given me reasons to be interested beyond having another camera on my face, hence why it’s one of the last features I got around to detailing.

The frame selection makes the idea of wearing these every day more appealing. Gemini offers a potentially useful connection between what I’m seeing and the apps I use. And translation gave me a glimpse of an experience I’d actively want to repeat.

For now, the conversation about Shenzhen is what I keep coming back to. For a few minutes, I was thinking more about the person in front of me than the technology that was making our conversation possible.

If Google can deliver more smart glasses experiences that feel invisible rather than invasive, it could be exactly the boost this category desperately needs right now.
